Small, oval brown spots appear on leaves, often in weak soil. Fix this by improving soil health with balanced fertilizers (NPK) and Zinc. If the infection is heavy, spray Mancozeb (2g/liter) or Edifenphos (1ml/liter). Soaking seeds in hot water (52°C) for 10 minutes before planting can kill hidden spores. It is often a "disease of the poor soil," so good manuring helps prevent it.

This causes long, wavy yellow-white streaks from leaf tips. It spreads fast in wind and rain. There is no easy cure, but spraying Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (20g) helps slow it down. Reduce Nitrogen levels and drain the field for a few days to stop bacteria from moving through the water to healthy plants.

Look for greenish-grey "snake-skin" patches on leaf sheaths near the water line. It loves crowded, wet fields. To treat, spray Hexaconazole (2ml/liter) or Validamycin (2ml/liter) directly at the base of plants where the stem meets the water. Keep the field free of weeds and avoid planting too closely; wider spacing allows air to dry out the dampness.

Grains turn into large, velvety orange-to-black "smut balls" during flowering in cool, rainy weather. Once balls appear, they cannot be cured. Prevention is key: spray Copper Oxychloride (2.5g/liter) or Propiconazole (1ml/liter) during the "booting" stage (just before grain-heads emerge). Remove and burn any smut balls seen to prevent the fungus from staying in the soil.

This rots the leaf sheath covering the young grain-head, stopping it from coming out fully. It usually happens when insects wound the plant. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter) or Mancozeb (2g/liter) at the "booting" stage. Controlling stem borers and other insects is vital, as their bites create the entry points for this fungus to infect the plant from inside.

Plants turn orange-yellow and stop growing (stunted). This virus is spread by Green Leafhoppers. You cannot treat the virus itself, so you must kill the insects. Spray Imidacloprid (0.5ml/liter) or Thiamethoxam immediately. Pull out and bury infected yellow plants instantly. Using resistant varieties like Vikramarya is the most effective way to avoid this disease entirely.

Some plants grow much taller and thinner than others, eventually turning pale and dying. This is a seed-borne disease. The best treatment is seed soaking: treat seeds with Carbendazim (2g/kg) before sowing. If you see these "foolish" tall seedlings in the field, pull them out carefully and destroy them so they don’t spread the fungus into the soil for next year.

Small black spots appear on the leaf sheath at the water level; later, the stem rots and the plant falls over. Draining the water and letting the soil crack for a few days can stop the fungus from spreading. Apply extra Potassium (Potash) to strengthen the stem walls. If severe, drench the base of plants with Thiophanate-methyl (1g/liter) to protect the stem.

scientific_name: Alternaria spp., Curvularia spp., Fusarium spp.
treatment: Grains turn black, red, or dark brown, making them look dirty and reducing market price. This is caused by various germs attacking during the "milky" stage. To prevent this, spray a combination of Mancozeb and Carbendazim (2g/liter) when grains are just forming. Ensure the field is free of weeds, as they act as a home for these germs between seasons.

This is a nutritional problem, not a germ. Spray Zinc Sulphate (5g) mixed with Lime (2.5g) in 1 liter of water as soon as you see dusty brown spots. For a 1-acre field, use 2kg Zinc Sulphate with 1kg Lime in 400 liters of water. For future crops, apply Zinc Sulphate (25kg per hectare) directly into the soil during land preparation.

This appears as fine, transparent streaks between leaf veins. Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (20g). Avoid excess Nitrogen, which makes leaves soft and easy to infect. Keep water levels low and avoid moving through the field while plants are wet to prevent spreading the bacteria on your clothes or tools to healthy areas.
Spray Hexaconazole or Propiconazole immediately.

You will see thin, short brown lines on the leaves. It usually happens in soils lacking Potassium. To treat, spray Propiconazole (1ml/liter) or Mancozeb (2g/liter) at the booting stage. The best long-term solution is to ensure you apply enough Muriate of Potash (MOP) during the early stages of the crop to make the plants naturally resistant.

Caused by tiny worms in the soil. Apply Carbofuran 3G granules (10-12 kg per acre) into the standing water. After harvesting, burn the left-over stubble or plow the field deeply during summer to kill the worms hiding in the soil. Rotating your crop with non-cereal plants like pulses for one season will starve the worms and clean the field naturally.

The grain-head comes out looking like a thin, silvery-white "candle" instead of grains. This lives inside the seed, so treat seeds with hot water (52°C) or Carbendazim (2g/kg) before planting. If you see "candle" heads in the field, pull them out carefully and bury them immediately so the black powder doesn't blow onto healthy plants or infect the soil.

Leaf tips look bleached or "scalded" with brown wavy bands. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter) at the first sign. Avoid heavy Nitrogen doses, especially in the rainy season. Ensure enough space between plants for air to flow; crowded plants stay wet longer, which helps this fungus spread. Proper drainage and balanced nutrition are the best ways to keep the leaves healthy.

A few grains turn into a black, powdery mass. It is hard to "cure" once visible. Prevent it by treating seeds with Carboxin or Carbendazim (2g/kg) before sowing. Spraying Propiconazole (1ml/liter) when the "boot" leaf is visible protects emerging grains. Avoid heavy irrigation and high Nitrogen during flowering, as moisture and soft growth encourage this disease to take hold.

You will see small, circular spots with light grey centers and dark red-brown borders. To treat, spray Mancozeb (2g/liter) or Carbendazim (1g/liter). If the leaves start falling off, ensure you remove and burn them. Avoid overhead watering, as splashing water spreads the fungal spores to healthy leaves.

This appears as a white, flour-like powder on the underside of leaves, while the top shows yellow patches. In dry, warm weather, it spreads fast. Spray wettable Sulfur (3g/liter) or Dinocap (1ml/liter). A home remedy is a mixture of baking soda and water (5g/liter). Ensure good spacing for better airflow between plants.

Look for small, water-soaked dark spots that eventually turn brown and "warty." Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter). Use disease-free seeds and avoid working in the field when plants are wet. Rotate crops so you aren't planting peppers or tomatoes in the same spot every year.

The leaves curl upwards, become small, and look "crinkled" or leathery. This is spread by tiny whiteflies. You cannot "cure" the virus, so focus on the insects. Spray Neem oil (5ml/liter) or Imidacloprid (0.5ml/liter). Install yellow sticky traps (15 per acre) to catch whiteflies. Pull out and bury infected plants immediately.

This causes large, dark-brown water-soaked patches on the leaves and leads to sudden wilting. It usually strikes during heavy rains. To treat, spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2g/liter). Improve your field's drainage immediately so water doesn't stand. Use raised beds for planting to keep the "collar" of the plant dry and safe from soil fungus.

The leaves show a "mosaic" pattern of light and dark green patches. This is spread by aphids or through touch. Control aphids using sticky traps and Neem spray. Always wash your hands and tools with soap after touching a sick plant. There is no chemical cure; infected plants must be removed and destroyed to save the rest.

It starts as small black spots on leaves and causes the branch tips to dry up like they are dying back. Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter) or Azoxystrobin (1ml/liter). Use healthy seeds and treat them with Trichoderma before sowing. Keep the field clean and ensure you aren't over-fertilizing with Nitrogen.

Small, circular spots with white centers and tiny black dots (spores) inside them. This can cause the plant to lose all its leaves. Spraying Chlorothalonil (2g/liter) or Mancozeb (2.5g/liter) works very well. Remove the infected lower leaves by hand and improve air circulation by pruning extra branches near the bottom of the plant.

A fuzzy grey mold grows on leaves, stems, or flowers during cool, damp weather. It enters through wounds. The best treatment is airflow—prune your plants and keep them spaced out. If it spreads, spray Carbendazim (1g/liter). Avoid high humidity by using drip irrigation instead of overhead sprinklers.

Young leaves turn bronze and develop small, dark spots or rings. Spread by tiny insects called Thrips. Control Thrips using blue sticky traps and by spraying Fipronil or Spinosad. Keep the field borders free of weeds where thrips hide. Once a plant is infected, it cannot be cured and should be removed.

Leaves wilt quickly as a white, "cottony" mold grows on the stem at the soil line. It looks like small mustard seeds are stuck to the stem. Deep plow the field in summer to bury the fungus. Solarise the soil with plastic sheets. Drench the base of the plants with a Trichoderma solution to protect the roots and stem.

The lower leaves turn yellow and the plant wilts, often on just one side first. Since this is in the soil, sprays don't help much. Drench the soil with Carbendazim (2g/liter). Mixing Trichoderma into your compost before planting is the best organic prevention. Ensure your soil isn't constantly soggy, as the fungus loves wet roots.
Control mites with Fenazaquin. Destroy infected plants.

Also called Botrytis. You will see grey, fuzzy mold on berries, usually after rain. Improve airflow by spacing plants well and weeding. Pick and bury rotting fruit immediately so spores don't spread. Avoid overhead watering. If rain is heavy during flowering, spray Cyprodinil + Fludioxonil (Switch), but keeping plants dry and mulched is the most effective cure.

Leaves curl upward like a cup and show white powdery dust underneath. This happens in humid conditions. Spray wettable Sulfur (2g/liter) or a baking soda solution (5g/liter) to change the leaf surface pH. If growing in a polyhouse, open vents to lower humidity. Ensure sunlight reaches the inner leaves to keep the plant dry.

Black, sunken spots appear on fruit; it can also kill runners. It spreads via infected nursery plants or splashing rain. Use disease-free seedlings. Use drip irrigation to stop water splashing soil spores onto fruit. Mulch with straw/plastic to create a barrier between fruit and soil. Spray Copper Oxychloride or Mancozeb if spots appear on runners.

Small purple spots with white/grey centers on leaves. It attacks older leaves first. Remove and burn these infected leaves to lower the disease load. Spray Copper-based fungicides (2g/liter) or Mancozeb. Do not work in the field when plants are wet, as your clothes can carry the fungus from sick to healthy plants.

Irregular purple or brown spots without white centers. Eventually, the leaves look "scorched" or burnt and dry up. It spreads by splashing water. The treatment is similar to Leaf Spot: remove old debris and apply fungicides like Captan or Thiram. keeping the plant vigorous with good nutrition helps it resist this infection better than weak plants.

Large, V-shaped brown spots start from the leaf edge and move inward. It often happens after harvest. Sanitate the field by removing old leaves. If the infection is severe, spray with Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl. Since this fungus survives on dead leaves in winter, cleaning your field at the end of the season is the best prevention.

The plant looks stunted and wilts even with water. If you cut the root, the core is rusty red (not white). It thrives in waterlogged soil. There is no cure; remove infected plants. Prevention is key: plant on raised beds (15cm high) for drainage. Dip new roots in Metalaxyl solution before planting.

The entire plant collapses suddenly. Cutting the crown (the thick stem base) reveals reddish-brown rot inside. Avoid over-watering and heavy soils. Use Fosetyl-Aluminium (Aliette) as a drench if permitted in your area. Use certified disease-free transplants, as this often comes from the nursery. Do not plant strawberries in low spots where water collects.

Fruit becomes hard, brown, leathery, and tastes bitter. This happens when fruit touches wet soil or mud splashes on it. The best fix is a physical barrier: use a thick layer of straw mulch or plastic so berries never touch dirt. Harvest ripe fruit quickly. If heavy rains are forecast, protect with a Captan spray beforehand.

Older outer leaves turn brown and dry while inner leaves stay green. The fungus stays in soil for years. Do not plant strawberries where you recently grew tomatoes, potatoes, or brinjal. If soil is infected, use Soil Solarisation (covering wet soil with clear plastic in hot summer) to cook the fungus. There is no chemical cure for infected plants.

Plants wilt rapidly, and roots turn dark brown/black. It loves warm weather (above 25°C). Since this is a soil-borne fungus, chemical sprays on leaves won't help. Drench soil with Trichoderma viride bio-fungicide regularly to protect roots. Solarise the soil before planting. If a plant dies, remove it with a shovel of soil surrounding it to remove the fungus.

This is not one disease but a mix of fungi, nematodes, and poor soil health. Roots turn black and rot. It happens in compacted, old soil. Improve soil aeration by adding organic matter (compost). Rotate crops every 2-3 years. Do not replant strawberries in the same spot immediately. Use bio-agents like Trichoderma and Pseudomonas to boost root health.

Small, water-soaked spots on the underside of leaves that look translucent when held up to light. Later they turn brown. Since this is bacterial, fungicides don't work well. Avoid overhead sprinklers completely. Spray Copper Hydroxide to limit spread. Do not harvest or prune when plants are wet.

Plants wilt during the day and recover at night, eventually dying. A milky ooze comes out if you cut the stem and put it in water. There is no cure. Remove and burn infected plants. Control weeds strictly. Rotate with mustard or marigold crops to suppress soil bacteria naturally. Ensure your tools are sterilized with bleach between rows.

Plants look stunted, and leaves may have uneven yellow patches, but symptoms are often unclear. It is spread by aphids. You cannot cure a virus. Control aphids using sticky traps and Neem oil sprays. Always buy "certified virus-free" plants from a lab or nursery. Remove any plant that looks dwarf or sickly immediately.

The side of the pumpkin touching the ground turns brown and dry/corky. This happens in very hot, humid weather. Use plastic mulch or a thick layer of dry straw to keep the pumpkin from touching the soil.

Leaves look crinkled, distorted, or have yellow spots. Also spread by aphids. The management is the same as other viruses: strict insect control. Keep the field border clean of weeds where aphids hide. If you see one infected plant, assume nearby plants might have it too and monitor them closely.

The flower petals turn into small green leaves, and the fruit looks woody. This is caused by phytoplasma spread by Leafhoppers. It looks strange but is serious. Pull out infected plants immediately. Control leafhoppers with appropriate insecticides (like Imidacloprid) or sticky traps. Keep the area free of weeds which host the hoppers.

Plants are weak/stunted. Roots have swollen "knots" or galls. Plant African Marigold flowers thickly between rows or as a rotation crop; their roots release chemicals that repel nematodes. Apply Neem Cake (200kg/acre) to the soil before planting. Use bio-nematicides like Paecilomyces lilacinus mixed with manure.

A white, grey, or yellow slimy coating appears on leaves or stems. It looks scary but actually doesn't hurt the plant much; it just sits on top. It usually goes away when the weather dries. You can wash it off with a strong jet of water. No chemical treatment is usually needed. Improve airflow to prevent it.

Berries develop pale, bleached patches where the hot sun hits them. This isn't a disease but heat damage. Ensure the plant has good leaf cover to shade the berries. In extreme heat, use shade nets (30% shade). Water frequently to keep the plants cool during peak afternoon heat.

Fruit looks puffed and stays white/pink instead of turning red, and tastes bland. This happens due to too much Nitrogen fertilizer or cloudy weather during ripening. Reduce Urea/Nitrogen application during fruiting. Supplement with Potassium and Calcium to improve fruit color and firmness.

Fruit is deformed, twisted, or has a "nub" end. This is caused by poor pollination (lack of bees) or frost damage during flowering. Avoid using strong pesticides during bloom so you don't kill bees. If frost is expected, cover plants with row covers. Boron deficiency can also cause this, so a foliar Boron spray may help.

White flour-like patches on leaves. Spray Hexaconazole (2ml/liter) or wettable Sulfur (3g/liter). For an organic fix, use a baking soda spray (5g/liter). Avoid overcrowding to let sunlight reach the inner leaves.

Yellow angular patches on top with grey "fuzz" underneath. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2g/liter). Avoid overhead watering; drip irrigation is best. Ensure proper spacing to help leaves dry quickly after rain.

Water-soaked spots that ooze a reddish-brown "gum" from stems. Spray Thiophanate Methyl (1g/liter) or Mancozeb (2.5g/liter). Always use certified seeds and clean up all crop debris after harvest to stop the fungus from hiding in old vines.

Leaf veins turn bright yellow; leaves become small/deformed. Spread by Whiteflies. No cure—pull out and bury sick plants immediately. Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps and sprays of Imidacloprid (0.5ml/liter) or Neem oil.

Sunken dark spots on leaves and fruit. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter) or Mancozeb (2g/liter). Treat seeds with Thiram (3g/kg). Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet to prevent the spread of spores on tools.
Small water-soaked "square" spots that may fall out, leaving "shot holes." Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter). Rotate crops with non-cucurbits for 2–3 years.
Small brown spots with "target-like" rings. Spray Mancozeb (2.5g/liter). Plants lacking Potassium (Potash) are more vulnerable. Deep summer plowing helps kill spores hiding in the soil.

Whole plant wilts suddenly during the hot day. Drench the base with Carbendazim (2g/liter). Mix Trichoderma viride (2kg/acre) into your manure before planting. Improve drainage to prevent standing water.
Fruit touching wet soil turns soft with white "yeast-like" growth. Spray Metalaxyl (2g/liter). Grow pumpkins on mulch or raised beds. Remove and bury rotted fruits far away from the field.
Stunted/yellow plants; roots have small round "knots." Plant African Marigold as a border crop. Apply Neem Cake (250kg/acre) during land preparation. Use the bio-agent Paecilomyces lilacinus.
Small sunken spots on fruit that ooze a greenish-brown fluid. Spray Chlorothalonil (2g/liter). This loves cool, moist weather. Use disease-free seeds and avoid overhead irrigation.

Leaves look "bumpy," mottled green, and fruits are deformed with "warts." Spread by Aphids. No cure. Control aphids using yellow sticky traps and Neem oil. Keep the field free of weeds like milkweed which act as hosts.

A white "cottony" growth appears on stems or fruit, often with hard black "seeds" (sclerotia). Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter). This fungus survives in the soil for years. Rotate with non-susceptible crops like corn or wheat.

The bottom of the fruit (where the flower was) turns black and leathery. This is a Calcium deficiency caused by uneven watering. Maintain consistent soil moisture and apply Lime (Chuna) or a Calcium spray during fruit setting.

Flowers and young fruits are covered in "black-headed whiskers" and rot quickly. Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). This is very common during heavy monsoon rains. Removing spent flowers can help reduce the chance of rot.
Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb. Use resistant varieties.
Treat seeds with Thiram. Rotate crops.

Raised white, "chalky" blisters on leaf undersides and yellow patches on top. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2g/liter). Avoid overhead watering. Remove infected plants immediately to prevent the "white dust" spores from spreading.

Dark brown/black spots with "target rings" on leaves. Spray Mancozeb (2.5g/liter). This fungus loves high humidity. Ensure proper spacing and burn old plant debris after harvest to stop the fungus from hiding in the soil.

Pale yellow patches on top with grey/purple "fuzz" underneath. Spray Metalaxyl (2g/liter). Common in cool, damp weather. Use raised beds for drainage and avoid planting too early in the winter when dew is heavy.
Circular spots with grey centers and reddish-brown borders. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter). Thrives in hot, humid weather. Removing older, infected bottom leaves helps reduce the spread.

Yellow "V-shaped" patches on leaf edges; veins turn black. Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter). Use hot-water treated seeds (50°C for 30 mins) and avoid working in wet fields.
Leaves look "mosaic" (patchy green) and wrinkled. Spread by Aphids. No chemical cure. Control aphids with yellow sticky traps and Neem oil sprays. Pull out and bury infected plants immediately.

Leaves yellow on one side; plant wilts. Root shows a brown ring inside. Drench base with Carbendazim (2g/liter). Mix Trichoderma viride into compost before planting. Ensure soil is not too acidic (add Lime if needed).
Seedlings rot at the soil line and fall over. Treat seeds with Trichoderma (10g/kg) before sowing. Use raised beds and drench soil with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter) if rot appears.
Raised, "corky" or warty brown patches on radish skin. Common in dry, alkaline soils. Keep soil consistently moist during the first 4 weeks. Avoid adding fresh manure right before planting.
Plant wilts during the day; roots are swollen and deformed like "clubs." No easy cure. Increase soil pH by adding Lime (Chuna). Avoid planting radish in the same spot for at least 3 years.

Sunken, brown, dry lesions appear on the root near the soil line. Spray Thiophanate Methyl (1g/liter). Avoid deep planting and ensure the soil is well-aerated. Deep summer plowing is very effective in killing the fungus.

The root turns black, particularly at the point where side roots emerge. Caused by Aphanomyces. Spray Fenamidone + Mancozeb. This loves waterlogged, heavy soils. Improve drainage and rotate with non-cruciferous crops.

The root turns into a mushy, foul-smelling liquid. Usually starts from wounds. Avoid wounding roots during weeding. Ensure the field has no standing water. Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter) around the base.

The flowers turn into green leaf-like structures, and the plant becomes bushy. Spread by Leafhoppers. No cure. Control leafhoppers with Neem oil or Dimethoate. Pull out and destroy infected plants immediately.
While not a "disease," it causes internal browning or "brown heart" and cracked roots. Spray Borax (2g/liter) during the mid-growth stage. Common in sandy or over-limed soils.
Stunted/yellow plants; roots have "knots" or look hairy. Plant African Marigold as a border crop. Apply Neem Cake (250kg/acre) during land preparation.

The most dangerous disease. Look for spindle-shaped spots with grey centers on leaves. Spray Tricyclazole (0.6g/liter) or Carbendazim (1g/liter). If the "neck" or "earhead" turns black, spray immediately to save grains. Avoid over-using Urea; split your nitrogen doses. Use resistant seeds like GPU-28 or ML-365.

Small, oval, light-brown spots appear and can cover the whole leaf. Spray Mancozeb (2g/liter) as soon as spots appear. This fungus hides on seeds, so treat them with Thiram or Captan (3g/kg) before sowing. Rotating the crop with legumes (like pulses) helps clean the soil naturally.

Shows as long, narrow brown spots. Heavy infection makes leaves look "burnt." Spray Mancozeb (2g/liter) or Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). Ensure proper spacing between plants so sunlight can hit the lower leaves; sunlight is a natural killer for these fungal spores. Maintain soil fertility with organic manure.

Leaves turn pale yellow and look "shredded" or twisted. The grain head turns into a bunch of green leaves instead of seeds. There is no cure once it reaches the earhead. Pull out and burn infected plants immediately. Prevent it by treating seeds with Metalaxyl (4g/kg) and ensuring the field is well-drained.

Young seedlings turn brown and die shortly after emerging. This is a soil-borne fungus. Drench the nursery area with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter). To prevent it, always use raised beds for your nursery so water doesn't stand. Treat seeds with Trichoderma (10g/kg) to provide a biological shield against soil rot.

Large, irregular "bleached" patches appear on the leaves, looking like bands. It spreads fast in very humid weather. Spray Hexaconazole (2ml/liter) or Propiconazole (1ml/liter). Keep the field free of weeds and avoid planting too densely. This fungus loves high humidity, so keeping the area airy is your best defense.

Leaves show pale green or yellow streaks and a patchy appearance. The plant stays small and stunted. Spread by Aphids. You cannot cure the virus; you must kill the insects. Spray Neem oil (5ml/liter) or Dimethoate (1.7ml/liter). Pull out infected plants immediately to prevent the aphids from carrying the virus to healthy neighbors.

Fine, transparent, water-soaked streaks along the leaf veins that eventually turn brown. Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (20g). Avoid working in the field when plants are wet. Adding Potash (Potassium) to your fertilizer schedule helps the leaf develop a tougher skin against these bacteria.

While it affects grains, the first sign is often the darkening of the earhead tissues. Grains turn into green or black powdery sacs. Since it is seed-borne, seed treatment with Carbendazim (2g/kg) is the only effective way to stop it. If you see smutted heads, remove them carefully in a plastic bag and burn them.

Lower leaves turn yellow and the whole plant wilts and dries up. Drench the base of the plants with Carbendazim (2g/liter). The best prevention is to mix Trichoderma viride (2kg/acre) with compost and apply it to the soil before sowing. This beneficial fungus eats the disease-causing fungus in the ground.
Treat seeds with Carbendazim. Spray Mancozeb.
Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb. Use resistant varieties.
Spray Mancozeb or Iprodione. Sow early.

Look for spindle or "eye-shaped" spots with grey centers on the leaves. To treat, spray Tricyclazole (0.6g/liter) or Carbendazim (1g/liter). Avoid giving all your Urea fertilizer at once; splitting the dose keeps the leaves from becoming too soft and "juicy" for the fungus. Always treat seeds with Pseudomonas fluorescens before sowing to build early leaf strength.

This shows as yellow-to-white wavy streaks starting from the leaf tips. Since chemicals can't "cure" bacteria easily, spray a mix of Streptocycline (1g in 10L) and Copper Oxychloride (20g) to stop the spread. Reduce Nitrogen fertilizer immediately and drain the field water for 3 days. This stops the bacteria from swimming from one plant to the next through the water.

You will see small, dark brown oval spots that look like sesame seeds on the leaves. This usually happens in "hungry" or weak soil. To treat, spray Mancozeb (2g/liter). Long-term, you must improve soil health by adding Zinc and Potash. It is often called the "poor farmer’s disease" because it only attacks plants that aren't getting enough nutrition from the ground.

Large, greenish-grey "snake-skin" patches appear on the leaf sheaths and spread up to the leaf blades. Spray Hexaconazole (2ml/liter) or Validamycin (2ml/liter) directly at the base and on the affected leaves. Avoid planting too closely; wider spacing allows the wind to dry the leaves. Keep the field bunds clean of grass and weeds where the fungus hides.
Control Whiteflies. Use resistant varieties.

This is a nutrition problem where the young leaves turn yellow at the base and develop rusty brown spots. To fix it, spray a mixture of Zinc Sulphate (5g) and Lime (2.5g) per 1 liter of water. You will see the leaves turn green again in 7–10 days. For the next crop, make sure to apply 25kg of Zinc Sulphate per hectare directly into the soil.
Maggots develop inside fruits causing internal rot. Collect fallen fruits and bury deep in soil. Use methyl eugenol traps and bait sprays to reduce fly population.

Look for very thin, straight, transparent lines between the leaf veins that eventually turn brown. Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (30g). Just like Leaf Blight, this disease loves high Nitrogen. Ensure your field has good drainage and avoid walking through the crop when the leaves are wet, as the bacteria can stick to your clothes.

This shows as very short, narrow brown lines that look like pencil marks on the leaves. To treat it, spray Propiconazole (1ml/liter). This disease is a signal that your plant needs more Potassium. Applying Muriate of Potash (MOP) during the early growth stages thickens the leaf walls, making it much harder for the fungus to poke through and start an infection.

The tips of the leaves look bleached or "burnt" with wavy, water-soaked brown bands. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter) at the first sign of these marks. Avoid heavy Nitrogen doses during the rainy season. This fungus spreads when wet leaves rub against each other, so proper spacing and removing weeds that keep the field too humid are the best ways to prevent it.

The leaves turn a distinct orange-yellow color from the tip downwards, and the plant stops growing. You cannot treat the virus itself, so you must kill the Green Leafhoppers that carry it. Spray Imidacloprid (0.5ml/liter) immediately. If you see only a few yellow plants, pull them out and bury them deep in the mud so the insects don't spread the virus further.

You will see bright red or orange-brown stripes running along the length of the leaf. This usually happens after heavy rains or high winds. To treat, spray Copper Oxychloride (2.5g/liter). Since this is a bacterial infection, avoid using too much Urea, which makes the stripes grow faster. Ensure the field is not overcrowded so the leaves can dry out quickly after it rains.

Small, slightly raised black spots appear on both sides of the leaf, looking like tiny specks of charcoal. It usually doesn't kill the plant but reduces the leaf's ability to make food. Spraying Mancozeb (2g/liter) or Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter) can control it. It is most common in shaded areas of the field, so ensure your crop gets plenty of direct sunlight.

Yellow angular spots on top of leaves with grey "fuzz" underneath. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2g/liter). Avoid overhead watering. Growing vines on a Mandap (trellis) is the best way to keep leaves dry and stop the spread.

White, flour-like patches on both sides of the leaf. Spray Hexaconazole (2ml/liter) or wettable Sulfur (3g/liter). A home remedy of baking soda (5g/liter) also works. Avoid over-using Nitrogen, which makes leaves soft and easy to infect.

Patchy yellow patterns on wrinkled leaves; plant stays stunted. Spread by Whiteflies. No cure—pull out sick plants immediately. Control whiteflies with yellow sticky traps and sprays of Imidacloprid (0.5ml/liter) or Neem oil.

Leaves look "mottled" (mixed light/dark green) and distorted. Spread by Aphids. No chemical cure. Kill aphids using Neem oil or yellow sticky traps. Keep field borders free of weeds where aphids and the virus hide.

Leaves turn yellow from the bottom up, and the whole vine wilts suddenly. Drench the base with Carbendazim (2g/liter). Mix Trichoderma viride into your manure before planting. Use raised beds to prevent waterlogging.

Water-soaked yellow spots on leaves and sunken black spots on fruit. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter). Treat seeds with Thiram (3g/kg). Avoid working in the field when leaves are wet to prevent the spread of spores.

Small circular spots with grey centers and dark margins. Spray Mancozeb (2g/liter). This loves high humidity. Pruning older bottom leaves improves airflow. Ensure the trellis is high enough to keep leaves off the soil.
Seedlings in the nursery rot at the soil line and fall over. Treat seeds with Trichoderma (10g/kg) before sowing. Use raised beds and drench soil with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter) if rot appears.

Fruit touching wet ground develops white "cottony" growth and rots. Spray Metalaxyl (2g/liter). The most effective fix is using a Trellis system so fruit never touches the soil. Bury rotted fruits far away.
Small, water-soaked "square" spots that may fall out, leaving "shot holes." Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter). Rotate crops with non-gourds for 2 years.
Small sunken spots on fruit that ooze greenish fluid; also causes "shot holes" in leaves. Spray Chlorothalonil (2g/liter). Loves cool, moist nights. Avoid planting too early in winter.
Water-soaked spots on leaves and stems that ooze reddish-brown "gum." Spray Thiophanate Methyl (1g/liter). Use healthy, certified seeds and remove all old vines after harvest.
Brown to black rotting patches appear on mature fruits, especially during rains. Remove infected fruits and maintain orchard hygiene. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter.
The side of the fruit touching the ground turns brown and corky. This happens in hot, humid weather. Use a trellis or place dry straw/mulch under fruits if they must grow on the ground.

Flowers and young fruits are covered in "black-headed whiskers" and rot quickly. Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). Very common during heavy monsoon. Removing spent flowers helps reduce the chance of rot.
Small brown spots with "target-like" rings. Spray Mancozeb (2.5g/liter). Usually attacks plants with poor nutrition. Ensure balanced NPK fertilizer to keep the vine's immune system strong.
Stunted/yellow plants; roots have small round "knots." Plant African Marigold as a border crop. Apply Neem Cake (250kg/acre) during land preparation.
Deep ploughing. Float seeds in salt water.
No cure. Remove infected trees immediately.

Yellow angular patches on top; purple-grey "fuzz" underneath. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2g/liter). Using a Trellis (Pandal) is essential. Avoid watering in the late evening so leaves don't stay wet overnight.
Green/yellow mottling and wrinkled leaves; twisted fruits. Spread by Aphids. No cure. Control aphids with yellow sticky traps and Neem oil (5ml/liter). Pull out and bury infected vines immediately.

White flour-like patches on leaves. Spray Hexaconazole (2ml/liter) or wettable Sulfur (3g/liter). Ensure the vine is not overcrowded; air must flow through the leaves to prevent this fungus from settling.
Water-soaked spots on stems that ooze reddish-brown "gum." Spray Thiophanate Methyl (1g/liter). Avoid wounding stems during weeding. Clean up old crop debris after harvest to kill hiding spores.
Sunken black spots on fruit and leaves. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter). Treat seeds with Thiram (3g/kg) before sowing. Avoid touching vines when they are wet with rain or dew.
Vine wilts suddenly; "milky thread" oozes from cut stems in water. No cure. Control Cucumber Beetles using Neem-based insecticides. Rotate with non-gourd crops like Corn or Millet.
Tips of long gourds turn soft and rot. Spray Metalaxyl (2g/liter). Ensure the Pandal is 6-7 feet high so gourds hang freely. Remove and bury rotted fruits far from the field.
Small circular spots with grey centers and purple borders. Spray Mancozeb (2g/liter). Pruning older, lower leaves improves sunlight penetration and reduces moisture.
Leaves yellow from base; plant wilts in the heat. Soil-borne. Drench base with Carbendazim (2g/liter). Mix Trichoderma viride into manure at planting time.
Weak/yellow vines; roots have "knots." Apply Neem Cake (250kg/acre) during land preparation. Planting Marigolds at the base of the trellis helps kill these worms.
Flowers and young fruits covered in "black-headed whiskers." Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). Common in heavy rain. Removing dead flowers from the tips of young fruits can stop the rot.

The lower stem turns dark brown or black and the plant wilts. Tiny black dots appear under the bark. Drench with Carbendazim. This loves hot, dry soil followed by heavy rain. Use mulch to keep soil temperature steady.
Causes severe "bumpy" distorted fruit and extreme yellowing. Spread by Aphids. No cure. This is more aggressive than common mosaic. Maintain strict aphid control from day one of planting.
The vine rots right at the soil level, often showing white "silk-like" fungal threads. Drench with Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). Avoid mounding wet soil directly against the main stem.

The tip of the fruit turns black and leathery (without mushy rot). This is a Calcium deficiency caused by irregular watering. Ensure steady moisture and spray Calcium Nitrate (5g/liter) during fruit formation.

Long gourds split open on the sides. Usually caused by heavy rain or sudden heavy irrigation after a dry spell. Maintain consistent soil moisture. Avoid heavy Nitrogen doses during the peak fruiting stage.
Yellow irregular spots on top; purplish-grey "fuzz" underneath. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2g/liter). Avoid evening watering; leaves must be dry at night. Use wider spacing for air circulation.
Small circular spots with white/grey centers and dark reddish borders. Spray Carbendazim (1g/liter) or Mancozeb (2g/liter). Removing older bottom leaves stops the fungus from jumping to new growth.
Small water-soaked spots that turn brown and thin like paper. Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). Ensure good drainage to prevent soil splashing onto leaves. Use healthy, disease-free seeds.
Young seedlings rot at the base and fall over. Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride (4g/kg) before sowing. Drench soil with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter) if rot appears. Use raised beds.

Leaves turn yellow; the whole plant wilts. Roots look dark or rotted. Soil-borne. Drench with Carbendazim (2g/liter). Best fix: mix Trichoderma into compost before planting. Rotate crops every 2-3 years.
Patchy green/yellow "mosaic" patterns; wrinkled leaves. Spread by Aphids. No cure. Control aphids with yellow sticky traps and Neem oil (5ml/liter). Pull out and bury infected plants immediately.
White "chalky" blisters on the leaf underside. Spray Metalaxyl (2g/liter). If seen, harvest healthy leaves immediately and destroy infected ones. Avoid overhead sprinklers.
Grey-to-tan circular spots that make leaves look "burnt." Spray Propiconazole (1ml/liter). Often confused with heat stress. Ensure plants have enough Potassium to strengthen leaf edges.
Small, water-soaked greasy spots that turn brown. Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10L) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (2g/liter). Avoid high-pressure sprays that wound the leaf skin.
Small, round, dark green "fuzzy" spots on both sides of the leaf. Spray Mancozeb (2.5g/liter). Happens in cool, wet conditions. Never harvest when plants are wet.
Roots turn black and "slimy," and the plant stays stunted. Drench soil with Metalaxyl (2g/liter). This loves waterlogged soil. Improve drainage and avoid over-irrigating during the monsoon.
Small brown spots that develop tiny black dots in the center. Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). Clean up all crop residue after harvest as the fungus hides in dead leaves.
Large, dark, mushy patches on leaves during very heavy rain. Spray Mancozeb. Best managed by using a temporary plastic rain shelter over the crop during peak monsoon.

One side of the leaf or plant turns yellow and wilts. Soil-borne. There is no chemical cure. Avoid planting in soil where potatoes or tomatoes were recently grown. Use Trichoderma at the time of sowing.
The edges of the leaves turn brown and dry. This is a Calcium deficiency caused by high heat or irregular watering. Maintain steady moisture and spray a Calcium-based micronutrient if needed.

New leaves are bright yellow, but the veins stay dark green. Spray Ferrous Sulfate (2g/liter). Common in alkaline (high pH) soils. Adding organic manure helps lower the pH and release Iron to the plant.

scientific_name: Sponge gourd yellow vein mosaic virus
treatment: Similar to Okra, the veins turn bright yellow while the rest of the leaf remains green. Spread by Whiteflies. Treatment: No cure. Pull out infected plants. Prevention: Install yellow sticky traps (15/acre) and spray Neem Oil (5ml/liter) or Acetamiprid early in the morning to kill whiteflies.

A thick white mold grows around the base of the stem at the soil line. You will see small, round, brown structures (sclerotia) that look like mustard seeds. Treatment: Drench the base with Hexaconazole (2ml/liter). This fungus loves high humidity and heavy manure. Ensure the soil around the stem is well-aerated.

The plant produces many tiny, crowded leaves instead of normal vines, looking like a "broom." Spread by Leafhoppers. Treatment: No cure. Pull out and destroy the plant. Prevention: Control leafhoppers using Dimethoate (2ml/liter). Keeping the field free of wild weeds like Parthenium (Congress grass) is vital as they harbor the phytoplasma.

The stem turns black and mushy, especially near the joints (nodes). This usually happens during the height of the rainy season. Treatment: Spray Carbendazim + Mancozeb (2g/liter). Avoid over-application of Urea, which makes the stems soft and juicy, attracting this fungus.
Use disease-free seeds. Spray Propiconazole at heading.

A black, powdery layer covers the leaves. This is not a direct disease but a fungus growing on the sticky "honeydew" left by Aphids or Mealybugs. Treatment: Kill the insects first. Once the insects are gone, the mold will dry up and wash off with water. The mold hurts the plant by blocking sunlight.

The roots and lower stem turn dark brown, and the bark can be easily peeled off to reveal tiny black specks. The plant wilts suddenly. Treatment: Drench the soil with Carbendazim (2g/liter). This disease thrives in "heat stress"—when the soil is very hot and dry, then suddenly becomes wet. Mulching helps keep soil temperatures steady.

The flowers turn yellow and fall off before fruit can form. Treatment: This is often caused by a lack of Micronutrients or very high temperatures. Spray a Micronutrient Mix (2g/liter) containing Boron and Zinc. Also, ensure there are enough bees in the field for pollination; avoid spraying pesticides during the daytime when bees are active.

The sponge gourd develops a very bitter taste. Treatment: This is caused by high levels of "Cucurbitacins," triggered by drought stress or sudden high heat. Maintain a consistent watering schedule and ensure the soil is rich in organic matter to buffer the plant against heat.

Also called Botrytis. You will see grey, fuzzy mold on berries, usually after rain. Improve airflow by spacing plants well and weeding. Pick and bury rotting fruit immediately so spores don't spread. Avoid overhead watering. If rain is heavy during flowering, spray Cyprodinil + Fludioxonil (Switch), but keeping plants dry and mulched is the most effective cure.

Leaves curl upward like a cup and show white powdery dust underneath. This happens in humid conditions. Spray wettable Sulfur (2g/liter) or a baking soda solution (5g/liter) to change the leaf surface pH. If growing in a polyhouse, open vents to lower humidity. Ensure sunlight reaches the inner leaves to keep the plant dry.

Black, sunken spots appear on fruit; it can also kill runners. It spreads via infected nursery plants or splashing rain. Use disease-free seedlings. Use drip irrigation to stop water splashing soil spores onto fruit. Mulch with straw/plastic to create a barrier between fruit and soil. Spray Copper Oxychloride or Mancozeb if spots appear on runners.

Small purple spots with white/grey centers on leaves. It attacks older leaves first. Remove and burn these infected leaves to lower the disease load. Spray Copper-based fungicides (2g/liter) or Mancozeb. Do not work in the field when plants are wet, as your clothes can carry the fungus from sick to healthy plants.

Irregular purple or brown spots without white centers. Eventually, the leaves look "scorched" or burnt and dry up. It spreads by splashing water. The treatment is similar to Leaf Spot: remove old debris and apply fungicides like Captan or Thiram. keeping the plant vigorous with good nutrition helps it resist this infection better than weak plants.

Large, V-shaped brown spots start from the leaf edge and move inward. It often happens after harvest. Sanitate the field by removing old leaves. If the infection is severe, spray with Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl. Since this fungus survives on dead leaves in winter, cleaning your field at the end of the season is the best prevention.

The plant looks stunted and wilts even with water. If you cut the root, the core is rusty red (not white). It thrives in waterlogged soil. There is no cure; remove infected plants. Prevention is key: plant on raised beds (15cm high) for drainage. Dip new roots in Metalaxyl solution before planting.

The entire plant collapses suddenly. Cutting the crown (the thick stem base) reveals reddish-brown rot inside. Avoid over-watering and heavy soils. Use Fosetyl-Aluminium (Aliette) as a drench if permitted in your area. Use certified disease-free transplants, as this often comes from the nursery. Do not plant strawberries in low spots where water collects.

Fruit becomes hard, brown, leathery, and tastes bitter. This happens when fruit touches wet soil or mud splashes on it. The best fix is a physical barrier: use a thick layer of straw mulch or plastic so berries never touch dirt. Harvest ripe fruit quickly. If heavy rains are forecast, protect with a Captan spray beforehand.

Older outer leaves turn brown and dry while inner leaves stay green. The fungus stays in soil for years. Do not plant strawberries where you recently grew tomatoes, potatoes, or brinjal. If soil is infected, use Soil Solarisation (covering wet soil with clear plastic in hot summer) to cook the fungus. There is no chemical cure for infected plants.

Plants wilt rapidly, and roots turn dark brown/black. It loves warm weather (above 25°C). Since this is a soil-borne fungus, chemical sprays on leaves won't help. Drench soil with Trichoderma viride bio-fungicide regularly to protect roots. Solarise the soil before planting. If a plant dies, remove it with a shovel of soil surrounding it to remove the fungus.

This causes sunken, water-soaked spots on ripe fruit. It often happens when fruits touch the soil. Harvest fruit as soon as it ripens; do not leave it on the plant too long. Mulching (covering soil with straw/plastic) helps prevent soil spores from splashing onto the fruit. Spray Chlorothalonil (2g/liter) if severe.

Brown and grey rings appear on fruit touching the wet ground. It looks like a "buck's eye." Stake your plants to keep fruits off the soil. Mulching is the best prevention. Avoid flood irrigation that keeps the soil surface wet for too long. If needed, spray Copper Oxychloride.

This is not one disease but a mix of fungi, nematodes, and poor soil health. Roots turn black and rot. It happens in compacted, old soil. Improve soil aeration by adding organic matter (compost). Rotate crops every 2-3 years. Do not replant strawberries in the same spot immediately. Use bio-agents like Trichoderma and Pseudomonas to boost root health.

Small, water-soaked spots on the underside of leaves that look translucent when held up to light. Later they turn brown. Since this is bacterial, fungicides don't work well. Avoid overhead sprinklers completely. Spray Copper Hydroxide to limit spread. Do not harvest or prune when plants are wet.

Plants wilt during the day and recover at night, eventually dying. A milky ooze comes out if you cut the stem and put it in water. There is no cure. Remove and burn infected plants. Control weeds strictly. Rotate with mustard or marigold crops to suppress soil bacteria naturally. Ensure your tools are sterilized with bleach between rows.

Plants look stunted, and leaves may have uneven yellow patches, but symptoms are often unclear. It is spread by aphids. You cannot cure a virus. Control aphids using sticky traps and Neem oil sprays. Always buy "certified virus-free" plants from a lab or nursery. Remove any plant that looks dwarf or sickly immediately.

Leaves look crinkled, distorted, or have yellow spots. Also spread by aphids. The management is the same as other viruses: strict insect control. Keep the field border clean of weeds where aphids hide. If you see one infected plant, assume nearby plants might have it too and monitor them closely.

The flower petals turn into small green leaves, and the fruit looks woody. This is caused by phytoplasma spread by Leafhoppers. It looks strange but is serious. Pull out infected plants immediately. Control leafhoppers with appropriate insecticides (like Imidacloprid) or sticky traps. Keep the area free of weeds which host the hoppers.

Plants are weak/stunted. Roots have swollen "knots" or galls. Plant African Marigold flowers thickly between rows or as a rotation crop; their roots release chemicals that repel nematodes. Apply Neem Cake (200kg/acre) to the soil before planting. Use bio-nematicides like Paecilomyces lilacinus mixed with manure.

A white, grey, or yellow slimy coating appears on leaves or stems. It looks scary but actually doesn't hurt the plant much; it just sits on top. It usually goes away when the weather dries. You can wash it off with a strong jet of water. No chemical treatment is usually needed. Improve airflow to prevent it.

Berries develop pale, bleached patches where the hot sun hits them. This isn't a disease but heat damage. Ensure the plant has good leaf cover to shade the berries. In extreme heat, use shade nets (30% shade). Water frequently to keep the plants cool during peak afternoon heat.

Fruit looks puffed and stays white/pink instead of turning red, and tastes bland. This happens due to too much Nitrogen fertilizer or cloudy weather during ripening. Reduce Urea/Nitrogen application during fruiting. Supplement with Potassium and Calcium to improve fruit color and firmness.

Fruit is deformed, twisted, or has a "nub" end. This is caused by poor pollination (lack of bees) or frost damage during flowering. Avoid using strong pesticides during bloom so you don't kill bees. If frost is expected, cover plants with row covers. Boron deficiency can also cause this, so a foliar Boron spray may help.

Often called the "Cancer of Sugarcane." The plant dries up, and if you split the cane open, the inside is red with white cross-patches and smells like alcohol. Prevention is the only cure. Use resistant varieties (like Co 86032). Never plant seeds from a field that had Red Rot. Dip seed setts in Carbendazim (1g/liter) before planting. Rotate crops with rice or mustard for one season to break the cycle.

A long, black, dusty "whip" grows from the top of the plant. It looks like a burnt stick. Do not just cut it off! Gently cover the whip with a plastic bag before cutting it so the black dust (spores) doesn't fly onto other plants. Burn the bag. Remove the entire clump (roots and all). Treat seed setts with Propiconazole (1ml/liter) before sowing. Avoid keeping a "Ratoon" (second crop) if you had Smut.

The cane dries up and shrinks. If you cut it open, the center is hollow and light violet/brown. It usually happens when the plant is close to harvest. Avoid waterlogging; ensure your field drains well. Stop irrigation for a few weeks if you see wilting to reduce spread. Do not use seed from wilted fields. Apply Trichoderma viride (bio-fungicide) mixed with manure in the soil.

The top leaves get twisted, wrinkled, and shortened. White or yellow patches appear at the base of leaves. It often happens in the rainy season. It usually recovers on its own, but if severe, spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter) or Carbendazim (1g/liter). Adding micronutrients (Magnesium and Zinc) helps the plant recover faster.

You will see a white, powdery coating on leaves, looking like flour. It happens in dry, warm weather. Spray wettable Sulfur (3g/liter) or Karathane (1ml/liter). A home remedy is spraying a mixture of milk and water (1:9 ratio) or baking soda solution, which changes the leaf surface pH.

The plant produces many thin, small, white/yellow shoots at the base, looking like grass instead of cane. It will not produce any sugar. This is spread by aphids. Heat Treatment is the best cure: treat seed setts with hot water (50°C) for 2 hours before planting. Dig out and burn infected clumps immediately. Do not take a ratoon crop from an infected field.

The midrib (center vein) of the upper leaves turns bright yellow, while the rest of the leaf stays green. Cane growth slows down. It is spread by aphids. Use Tissue Culture seedlings (virus-free) for planting. Spray Imidacloprid (0.5ml/liter) to kill the aphids that spread it. Give the crop good fertilizer and water so it can tolerate the virus and still yield well.

This attacks the seed setts after planting. The inside of the sett turns black and smells like ripe pineapple. The buds fail to sprout. This happens if the cut ends of the seed are not treated. Always dip the cut ends of your seed setts in a solution of Carbendazim or Propiconazole for 15 minutes before planting to seal the wound.

White "pencil lines" run along the leaf veins. Later, the leaf dries up and looks scalded (burned by hot water). The cane may sprout side shoots. Use certified disease-free seeds. Sterilize your harvesting knives with bleach or by heating them, as the bacteria spreads through tools. Remove infected plants immediately.

Long, narrow red stripes appear on the leaves. If it moves to the top shoot, the top may rot (Top Rot) and smell bad. Since it is bacterial, fungicides won't work perfectly. Improve field drainage and avoid overhead sprinklers. You can spray Copper Oxychloride to limit the spread.

Small, elongated orange or brown spots appear on the leaves. If you touch them, orange powder comes off on your finger. It happens in cool, humid weather. Usually, the sun kills it as the weather warms up. If severe, spray Mancozeb (2g/liter) or Propiconazole (1ml/liter). Remove weeds that block sunlight from reaching the lower leaves.

Leaves show a pattern of dark and light green patches (mottling). The cane stalks may split. It is spread by aphids and infected knives. There is no chemical cure. Use resistant varieties. The most important step is roguing: check your field frequently and pull out any young plants showing these symptoms early in the season.

You won't see clear symptoms on leaves, but the plant simply doesn't grow tall. The yield drops significantly in the ratoon (second) crop. The inside of the nodes may have orange/red dots. The only prevention is Hot Water Treatment of seeds (50°C for 2 hours) and sterilizing cutting knives with Lysol or bleach between fields.

New leaves turn completely white or pale yellow/cream, but the veins might stay green. This is not a disease but a lack of Iron in the soil (common in calcareous/chalky soils). Spray Ferrous Sulphate (5g/liter) mixed with Citric Acid (1g/liter) on the leaves 2-3 times at 10-day intervals.
Spray Copper Oxychloride + Hexaconazole.
Spray Copper Oxychloride. Improve Potash nutrition.
Spray Thiamethoxam. Maintain shade.
Spray Quinalphos or Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt).
No cure. Remove plants. Wash hands (smokers carry virus).
Control Whitefly with Imidacloprid. Remove plants.

This kills young seedlings in the nursery. Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride (4g/kg) before sowing. Avoid over-watering the nursery bed; the soil should not be soggy. If you see rotting, drench the soil with Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). Use raised beds to help excess water drain away.

Look for brown spots with rings on older leaves. Spray Mancozeb (2g/liter) or Chlorothalonil (2g/liter) early in the morning. Remove and burn infected lower leaves to stop the upward spread. Rotate crops—do not plant tomatoes where you just grew potatoes or brinjals.

A fast-spreading rot during cloudy, wet weather. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb (2g/liter) or Cymoxanil (2g/liter) immediately at the first sign. Keep the field clean and avoid overhead sprinklers that wet the leaves. If it rains heavily, re-spray after the rain stops.

The plant yellows and dries up from one side. The fungus lives in the soil, so chemical sprays don't work well. Drench the soil around roots with Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter). The best fix is prevention: mix Trichoderma bio-fungicide with manure before planting and use resistant seeds.

Small round spots with grey centers on lower leaves. Remove infected leaves by hand to lower the fungal load. Spray Copper Oxychloride (3g/liter) or Mancozeb (2.5g/liter). Ensure good spacing between plants so air can flow through; crowded plants trap humidity and make this worse.

The plant droops and dies suddenly while still green. There is no chemical cure. Use wilt-resistant varieties (like Arka Abha). Dip seedling roots in Pseudomonas fluorescens before planting. Rotate crops with paddy (rice) or marigold to naturally clean the soil of bacteria.

Small, dark, greasy spots appear on leaves and fruits. It spreads by splashing rain. Avoid overhead watering. Spray Streptocycline (1g in 10 liters water) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (30g in 10 liters). Do not work in the field when plants are wet, as you will carry the bacteria to healthy plants.

Leaves turn brown at the edges ("firing") and stems may split open. Fruit may have small "bird-eye" spots. Use disease-free seeds from trusted sources. Sterilize your pruning tools (knives/scissors) with bleach solution between plants. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to save the rest.

Leaves curl upward and plants remain small. Spread by whiteflies. There is no cure for the virus. Pull out and bury infected plants instantly. Control whiteflies using yellow sticky traps (15/acre) and spray Imidacloprid (0.5ml/liter) or Neem oil to stop the spread.

Causes bronzing of young leaves and ring-spots on fruit. Spread by tiny insects called Thrips. Control Thrips using blue sticky traps and by spraying Fipronil or Spinosad. Keep the field borders free of weeds where thrips hide. Remove infected plants immediately.

Leaves show a light and dark green mosaic pattern. This is highly contagious and spreads by touch (smokers can spread it from tobacco!). Wash hands with soap before handling plants. Do not smoke near the field. Remove infected plants and do not compost them.

The bottom of the fruit turns black and flat. This is not a disease but a Calcium deficiency caused by uneven watering. Water regularly so the soil stays moist (not soaked). Spray Calcium Chloride (2g/liter) on the fruits when they are small (marble size).

cracks appear on the fruit skin. This happens when heavy rain follows a dry spell; the fruit drinks water too fast and bursts. maintain consistent soil moisture by watering regularly. Harvest fruits before heavy rains if they are close to ripening.

White/yellow patches on the fruit where the sun hit it too hard. This happens when leaves fall off due to other diseases. Keep the plant healthy so leaves cover the fruit. In severe summers, you can use shade nets or cover fruit clusters with straw.

Fruit becomes deformed and scarred. Caused by cold weather during flowering or high nitrogen fertilizer. Avoid planting too early in winter. Use balanced fertilizers; do not overuse Urea (Nitrogen) which causes rapid, weak growth.

Plants look weak and stunted; roots have swollen "knots" or galls. Plant African Marigold flowers between tomato rows (their roots release chemicals that repel nematodes). Apply Neem Cake (250kg/acre) to the soil. Use Paecilomyces lilacinus (bio-agent) in the soil.

A grey, fuzzy mold grows on dying flowers or fruit stem ends. It loves high humidity. The best treatment is airflow—prune extra leaves and keep spacing wide. Remove dead flowers that stick to the fruit. Spray Chlorothalonil only if necessary.

A white mold grows on the stem near the soil, looking like mustard seeds. The plant wilts quickly. Deep plow the field in summer to bury the fungus. Solarise soil (cover with plastic in summer). Drench the base of plants with Trichoderma.

Pale yellow spots on top of leaves, with olive-green mold underneath. Common in humid greenhouses. Improve ventilation immediately to lower humidity. Use drip irrigation instead of overhead sprays. Spray Copper-based fungicides if the infection spreads.
Drench soil with Copper Oxychloride. Use raised beds.
Spray Mancozeb or Carbendazim.
Control Whitefly with Thiamethoxam. Use resistant varieties.
Use virus-free seeds. Remove infected plants.
Spray Wettable Sulphur or Carbendazim.
Treat seeds with Trichoderma. Avoid drought.
Drench soil with Carbendazim. Avoid waterlogging.
Spray Copper Oxychloride + Streptocycline.
Spray Wettable Sulphur or Propiconazole.
Soft rot in wet weather. Avoid soil contact. Spray Mancozeb.
Dark sunken spots appear on ripening fruits causing soft rot. Prune trees to improve airflow and remove infected fruits. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during flowering and fruit set.
Fruits develop soft brown rot during humid weather. Improve drainage and avoid water stagnation. Remove infected fruits immediately. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit development.
Dark sunken lesions appear on fruit skin causing cracking. Prune overcrowded branches and improve air circulation. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during flowering.
Maggots develop inside fruits causing internal rot. Collect fallen fruits and bury deep in soil. Use pheromone traps and bait sprays to control flies.
Fruits soften and rot during rainy season. Harvest fruits on time and avoid leaving them on wet ground. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter if infection appears early.

This is a very common problem where the outer shell (hull) rots after it splits, often causing the nearby leaves and twigs to die. It is caused by too much nitrogen or water. To stop this, reduce irrigation and Nitrogen fertilizer slightly when the hulls start splitting (harvest time). Spray Iprodione or Boscalid fungicides at the early hull-split stage. Harvest early to prevent the fungus from producing poisons that kill the branches.

This fungus attacks the flowers and young nuts, turning them soft and brown. The infected nuts often stick to the branch and dry up (mummies). You must remove and destroy these "mummy" nuts during winter cleaning. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Tebuconazole @ 1 ml per liter when the flower buds turn pink and again at full bloom. If it rains during flowering, an extra spray is necessary.

Orange or rust-colored sunken spots appear on the young nuts. During wet weather, the nuts produce a lot of gum and may fall off. Prune out dead branches and remove infected nuts. Spray Azoxystrobin or Propiconazole @ 1 ml per liter during the pink bud stage and repeat every 10-14 days if rains continue during spring. This disease can kill the nut completely if not treated early.

Grey to black, oily-looking spots appear on the hulls (outer shells). If the infection is severe, the hull does not open properly, and the kernel inside remains small. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Ziram @ 2 grams per liter starting two weeks after the petals fall. Repeat the spray every 2 weeks until the shell hardens. Prune the tree to allow air to dry the nuts quickly after rain.

Small, water-soaked spots appear on the hull, which later produce amber-colored gum. This can damage the kernel inside causing it to look gummy or dark. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Bordeaux mixture (1%) during the dormant season (winter). Once leaves appear, use Ziram or Mancozeb instead of Copper to avoid burning the leaves.

This is the worst pest for almonds. The worm enters the nut after the hull splits and eats the kernel, leaving behind web and black waste. The most important step is "Winter Sanitation": knock down all old nuts (mummies) remaining on trees in winter and destroy them, as the worms hide there. Harvest as soon as 100% of hulls have split. Spray Spinosad or Methoxyfenozide at hull split if necessary.

You will see clear, jelly-like gum oozing from the nuts. When you cut the nut, the kernel inside has a dark spot or is dead. This is caused by bugs piercing the nut, not a fungus. Monitor the orchard for Leaffooted Bugs or Stink Bugs. Spray Permethrin or Bifenthrin if you see many bugs in the spring. Removing weeds around the orchard prevents these bugs from breeding near the trees.

The kernel inside the shell develops a grey or black mold, making it bitter and unsafe to eat. This usually happens if rain gets inside the split hull during harvest. Harvest the nuts as soon as they are ready; do not leave them on the tree after the hulls open. If rain is forecast during harvest, try to pick the nuts early. Dry the harvested nuts immediately to stop mold growth.
Dark irregular sunken spots appear on fruit skin. Prune overcrowded branches and spray Copper fungicide @ 3 grams per liter during early fruit stage.
Brown soft rot develops on fruits during rainy weather. Improve drainage and avoid fruit injuries. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit development.

Black, circular blisters or rings appear on the fruit skin, which spoils the look and quality of the fruit. To control this, spray Wettable Sulphur @ 3 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during the early fruiting stage. If the infection is severe, repeat the spray after 15 days. Always buy disease-free seedlings to prevent this from entering your orchard.

The fruit looks healthy from the outside, but when you cut it, the flesh inside is brown or black. This is not a fungus but caused by a lack of the nutrient Boron. To fix this, spray Borax @ 6 grams per liter of water. You should do this three times: once when flowers appear, again when fruits are pea-sized, and finally when fruits are half-grown.
Maggots develop inside fruits leading to early drop. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury deep. Use pheromone traps to reduce fly population.

This usually happens after harvest or if fruits get injured on the tree. The infected part turns soft, brown, and watery, sometimes with a blue-green mold. Handle fruits very gently during harvest to avoid cuts and bruises. Dip the harvested fruits in a weak salt solution (sodium chloride) or Borax solution (borax @ 1 gram per liter) to clean them and protect against rotting during storage.

A small caterpillar bores a hole into the fruit and eats the seed, causing the fruit to rot and fall. Collect and destroy all fallen, infested fruits to break the cycle. Spray Carbaryl @ 2 grams per liter or Quinalphos @ 2 ml per liter when fruits are starting to develop. You can also hang light traps to catch the moths that lay the eggs.

Brown, sunken spots appear on the fruit surface, which may join together to form large rotten patches. This is common in humid weather. Prune the tree to allow sunlight to reach the fruits. Spray Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during the fruit setting stage. Keep the ground clean of fallen leaves.

The fruit develops dark brown to black spots that become hard and dry. The skin may wrinkle. This often happens if the tree is weak. Ensure the tree gets enough water and fertilizer. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter or Chlorothalonil @ 2 grams per liter if you see spots appearing on young fruits.

Olive-green to black velvety spots appear on fruit skin, making it rough and cracked. Collect and destroy fallen leaves and fruits where fungus survives. Prune trees to allow sunlight and air flow. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter or Captan @ 2 grams per liter starting at green tip stage and repeat every 10–14 days during wet weather.

Young fruits turn black, shrivel, and hang on branches as if burned. Cut infected branches at least 12 inches below damage and burn them. Disinfect pruning tools after every cut. Spray Streptocycline + Copper Oxychloride during flowering if disease is common in the area.

Small brown sunken spots appear on fruit which enlarge and develop pink spore rings. Remove all mummified fruits from trees and ground. Spray Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or Thiophanate Methyl during fruit development in warm, humid weather.

Black smudges or tiny black dots appear on fruit skin, reducing market value but not internal quality. Prune canopy to reduce humidity. Spray Mancozeb or Zineb @ 2 grams per liter during late summer rains.
Worm bores into apple and feeds on seeds, leaving brown waste at entry hole. Collect and destroy fallen fruits. Install pheromone traps. Spray Spinosad @ 0.3 ml per liter after petal fall.

This is the most common disease where the fruit turns soft, brown, and gets covered in dusty grey fungal powder. The fruit rots completely and may dry up (mummify) on the branch. To stop this, you must pick and burn all the dried "mummy" fruits hanging on the tree during winter. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Tebuconazole @ 1 ml per liter when the flowers open and again 2 weeks before harvesting to protect the fruit from rotting.

Small, purple-red spots appear on the fruit skin, which later turn into rough, scabby bumps. The fruit looks spotted and ugly. This fungus lives in infected buds and twigs. Prune out dead wood and infected branches during winter. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Bordeaux Mixture (1%) just before the buds swell in spring and again after the petals fall to protect the young fruit.

Small, round, olive-green to black velvet spots appear on the fruit skin. These spots usually stay on the surface but make the fruit look dirty and reduce its price. It happens in damp, shady conditions. Prune the tree to let more sunlight reach the center. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter or Captan @ 2 grams per liter when the shucks (flower covers) fall off the young fruit. Repeat the spray after 15 days.

Dark, sunken spots appear on the fruit, often causing deep cracks and pits. Sticky gum may ooze out of these spots. This is harder to control than fungal diseases. Plant resistant varieties if possible. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during the dormant season (winter). Be careful using Copper after leaves appear as it can burn them; use agricultural antibiotics like Streptocycline only if recommended by local experts.

White powdery patches appear on the young green fruit. As the fruit grows, these spots disappear but leave behind hard, rusty-brown, rough patches (russeting) on the skin. To prevent this roughness, spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter or Myclobutanil @ 0.5 ml per liter as soon as the petals fall. Keep the orchard weed-free to reduce humidity.

Dark, reddish-purple rings or irregular blotches appear on the fruit surface. The fruit becomes bumpy and deformed. The flesh inside may have dead, brown streaks. There is no chemical spray to cure this virus. The only solution is to remove the infected tree to save the others. Use only certified virus-free saplings when planting new trees.

This rot hits the ripe fruit after harvest. The fruit turns very soft, watery, and develops a "whiskery" black mold. It enters through cuts and bruises. Handle apricots very gently; do not throw them into crates. Cool the fruit immediately after picking. Dip the fruit in a recommended post-harvest fungicide like Fludioxonil or simply maintain strict hygiene and cool storage temperatures.

These are insects, not a disease, but they cause damage that looks like rot. They hide in the clusters and chew holes in the ripening fruit, causing it to rot. Trap them by wrapping corrugated cardboard or damp newspaper around the tree trunk; the insects will hide there during the day, and you can remove and burn the traps. Keep the area around the tree trunk clean of weeds and debris.
Fruits soften and rot after harvest if injured. Handle fruits gently and store in cool conditions. Dip fruits in Carbendazim solution before storage.
Sunken dark lesions develop on fruits leading to cracking. Improve air circulation and spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit formation.

This is the most dangerous disease during the monsoon. Dark water-soaked spots appear on the nut surface near the cap, and the nuts rot and fall in large numbers. To control this, cover the bunches with polythene covers (Kotte) before the rains start to keep them dry. Spray Bordeaux Mixture (1%) just before the monsoon begins. If rains are heavy, repeat the spray after 45 days. Collect and burn all fallen, rotting nuts to stop the fungus from spreading.

The flower stalks and young buttons start drying from the tip backwards, turning dark brown or black. This causes severe shedding of baby nuts. Prune off the dried, infected parts of the bunch and burn them. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter or Chlorothalonil @ 2 grams per liter just after the female flowers open. Apply balanced fertilizers (Potash) to strengthen the tree against this drying.

Young nuts (buttons) fall off excessively without any obvious rot. This can be due to a lack of pollination or nutrients. Ensure your garden has proper drainage during the rainy season and irrigation during summer. Apply Borax @ 20 grams per tree mixed with soil. If shedding continues, spray NAA (Planofix) @ 1 ml in 5 liters of water on the opening bunches to help hold the nuts.

The nuts crack open while still on the tree, spoiling the quality. This is usually not a disease but happens when a long dry spell is followed by sudden heavy rain or over-watering. To prevent this, maintain constant soil moisture by watering regularly in summer and using mulch (dry leaves) at the tree base. Spray Borax @ 2 grams per liter on the bunches when nuts are developing. Improve drainage to remove excess water quickly.

A small bug punctures the tender nuts to suck sap. The nuts turn yellow, shrivel, and fall. If you look closely at fallen nuts, you will see tiny pin-prick holes. Spray Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter or Dimethoate @ 1.5 ml per liter on the young bunches. Keep the plantation clean of weeds where these bugs hide.

You will see sticky webs and frass (waste) on the flower bunch. The caterpillar bores into the nuts and flower stalks, causing them to dry. Open the bunches manually to clean out the webs and worms. Spray Malathion @ 2 ml per liter or Quinalphos @ 1.5 ml per liter when you first see the webbing. Using light traps at night can help catch the moths before they lay eggs.

The nuts exposed to the harsh afternoon sun (South-West side) turn golden yellow, develop cracks, and the kernel inside becomes black and hard. This is not a fungus but heat damage. Cover the exposed bunches with areca leaf sheaths or opaque polythene covers. Plant tall shade trees on the South-Western border of the garden to block the direct sun.

Dark sunken spots appear on fruit surface and later cause rotting after harvest. Handle fruits gently to avoid injuries. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during flowering and early fruit stage. Harvest fruits carefully and store in cool conditions.

Fruit rots from stem end during storage, turning brown and soft inside. Harvest fruits with short stalk intact. Avoid pulling fruits. Dip harvested fruits in Carbendazim solution @ 1 gram per liter and store in cool, dry place.
Raised corky brown spots appear on fruit skin, reducing appearance. Prune trees to improve airflow. Spray Copper fungicide @ 3 grams per liter during early fruit development.
Rough, brown scarring develops on fruit surface due to insect feeding. Monitor orchard regularly. Spray Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter or Spinosad if infestation is high. Maintain orchard hygiene.
White or yellow patches develop on fruit exposed to strong sunlight. Maintain good leaf cover by avoiding heavy pruning. Provide regular irrigation and balanced nutrition.
Black coating forms on fruit surface due to insect honeydew. Control aphids and scale insects using Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter. Wash fruits to remove mold.
Yellow spots on leaves; fruit quality drops. Spray Mancozeb. Avoid wet foliage.
Fruits rot internally due to maggots. Collect and destroy fallen fruits. Use bait traps and avoid overripe fruits on trees.
Fruit shell cracks due to irregular watering. Maintain steady soil moisture and avoid drought followed by heavy irrigation. Mulching helps reduce cracking.

Handle the fruit bunches carefully during harvest and transport to avoid any bruises or cuts, as this is where the rot starts. Remove and destroy any decaying leaves or infected fruits from the plantation. After harvesting, dip the banana hands in a Carbendazim solution (1 gram per liter) or hot water (50°C) for 5 minutes before storing to prevent the black spots from developing.

Immediately after the fruits have formed, manually remove the dried flower parts (pistils) hanging at the tip of the banana fingers, as these attract the fungus. Cover the bunches with polyethylene sleeves (bunch covers) to protect them. If you see the infection starting, spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2.5 grams per liter on the bunches.

scientific_name: Colletotrichum musae / Fusarium spp. / Lasiodiplodia theobromae
treatment: Keep your harvesting knives and tools very clean and sharp. Cut the banana hands leaving a clear portion of the crown (stalk) attached. Immediately after cutting, dip the cut ends of the crown in a solution of Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or apply a mixture of Alum and water to the cut surface. Allow the surface to dry completely before packing to stop the rot from entering the stalk.

This reddish-brown roughness on the skin is caused by tiny insects called thrips. Place blue sticky traps in the field to catch them. Cover the banana bunches with polythene bags as soon as the last hand opens to block the insects. If the attack is severe in the early stages, spray Imidacloprid @ 0.5 ml per liter or Dimethoate @ 2 ml per liter on the young bunches.

This rot often happens when fruits are damaged or sun-scorched. Maintain good shade in the garden and ensure proper drainage to avoid waterlogging. Remove and bury any rotting fruits far away from the field. When washing harvested bananas, use clean water mixed with a little chlorine (bleaching powder) to kill surface bacteria and dry the fruits well before packing.

Keep the plantation clean by removing weeds and grass where beetles hide. When the banana bunch starts forming, ensure the leaves do not touch the fruits, as beetles use leaves as bridges to reach the bunch. Bagging the bunches (covering with plastic) at the early shooting stage is the most effective method. You can also spray Chlorpyrifos @ 2.5 ml per liter on the young bunch once before bagging.

This bacterial disease causes the inside pulp to turn brown and dry even if the outside looks okay. Always use clean, sterilized tools for pruning and harvesting, as the bacteria spreads through knife blades.
