Small, round, velvet-black spots (freckles) appear on the fruit skin, mostly near the stem. In severe cases, these spots merge, forming large black patches that cause the fruit skin to crack. Prune the tree to open the center so sunlight reaches all fruits, as this fungus loves shade. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter or Captan @ 2 grams per liter starting two weeks after petals fall. Repeat every 10-14 days until the fruit is half-grown.

Small, angular, purple-black spots appear on the fruit, causing deep pits or cracks. Sticky gum often oozes out from these wounds. This is very hard to cure once it starts. The best solution is to plant resistant varieties. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Oxytetracycline during the early growing season, but be careful as Copper can burn peach leaves; use it only when recommended for your area.

This rot attacks ripe fruits during harvest or storage. The fruit turns very soft, watery, and leaks liquid. It gets covered in a fluffy white mold with tiny black dots. This fungus enters only through cuts and bruises. Handle peaches like eggs during harvest; do not drop or squeeze them. Cool the fruits immediately after picking. Clean the packing crates with bleach solution.

Circular, sunken brown spots appear on the fruit skin. In wet weather, you might see sticky, salmon-pink colored spores in the center of the spots. The fruit eventually rots. Remove wild plum or neglected fruit trees near your orchard as they carry this fungus. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Propiconazole @ 1 ml per liter during the fruit development stage, especially if the weather is warm and rainy.

White, powdery patches appear on young fruits. As the fruit grows, these spots turn into hard, russeted (rusty-brown) patches or net-like patterns on the skin. The fruit does not rot but looks bad and sells for less. Prune the tree to reduce humidity. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter or Myclobutanil @ 0.5 ml per liter when the fruit shucks (coverings) start splitting off.

A small beetle cuts a crescent-shaped (half-moon) mark on the fruit skin to lay eggs. The grub (worm) eats inside, causing the fruit to rot and drop early. Collect and destroy all dropped fruits immediately to kill the larvae inside. Spray Imidacloprid @ 0.5 ml per liter or Phosmet @ 1.5 grams per liter just after the petals fall to kill the adults before they lay eggs.
Bumpy, mottled, deformed fruits ("warty"). Remove plants. Control aphids.

The larvae bore into the fruit near the stem, feeding around the pit (stone). The entry hole is often filled with gummy waste. The fruit ripens too fast and rots. Use pheromone mating disruption ties in the orchard to confuse male moths. Spray Spinosad @ 0.3 ml per liter or Carbaryl @ 2 grams per liter if you see shoot wilting or fruit damage beginning in early summer.

The fruit looks fine from the outside, but when heated for canning or cooking, the flesh turns brownish-pink and smells bad. This is caused by bacteria. To prevent this, harvest the fruit early before it becomes over-ripe. Avoid harvesting during heavy rain. Ensure the field has good drainage and apply balanced fertilizers to keep the plant strong.

This fungus causes dark, velvety, olive-green spots on the fruit, which later become black, corky, and rough (scabby). The fruit often cracks and becomes deformed. To control this, collect and burn all fallen leaves and fruits in autumn as the fungus hides there during winter. Prune the tree to open up the canopy for sunlight. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2.5 grams per liter when the buds are just opening and again when small fruits are forming.

This is a dangerous bacterial disease where the young fruits turn black, shrivel, and dry up but stay hanging on the tree, looking like they were burned by fire. Usually, liquid oozes from the infected parts. Cut the infected branches 12 inches below the visible damage using shears dipped in bleach solution between every cut. Spray Streptocycline (0.5 gram) mixed with Copper Oxychloride (2 grams) per liter of water during the flowering stage to protect the young fruits.

Small, brown, circular spots appear on the fruit, which enlarge and sink into the flesh. In humid weather, pinkish spores appear in the center of the spots. The fruit tastes bitter and rots. Remove all "mummy" (dried) fruits hanging on the tree. Spray Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or Thiophanate Methyl @ 1 gram per liter during the summer when fruits are growing. Ensure good drainage in the orchard.

Small, purple-black spots appear on the fruit skin. As the fruit grows, the spots become sunken, and the fruit may crack or drop early. This happens mostly in wet seasons. Rake up and destroy fallen leaves and fruits. Spray Chlorothalonil @ 2 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter starting from petal fall. Repeat the spray every 10-15 days if the rain continues.

The fruit becomes extremely bumpy, pitted, and deformed. The flesh inside becomes hard and woody (stone-like) and is difficult to cut. This is a virus and cannot be cured by spraying chemicals. The only solution is to remove the infected tree so it does not infect others. Always use virus-free grafted plants from a certified nursery when planting new trees.

These are two different fungi that often appear together. Sooty blotch looks like black smudges on the skin, and flyspeck looks like tiny black dots (fly poop). It is a cosmetic issue and does not rot the fruit inside. Prune the tree to allow air circulation and reduce humidity around the fruits. Spraying Zineb or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during the late summer rains will easily clean up the skin.

This is the most common rot during storage. The fruit develops a soft, watery spot that quickly gets covered in blue-green powdery mold. It has a musty smell. Handle pears very gently during harvest to avoid punctures or bruises, as the mold enters through wounds. Dip harvested fruits in a solution of Thiabendazole before storage. Keep the storage area cool and clean.

The larva bores into the fruit and eats the seeds, pushing out brown waste (frass) through the entry hole. The fruit ripens early and falls. Scrape loose bark from the tree trunk where larvae hide during winter. Hang Pheromone traps to catch male moths. Spray Spinosad @ 0.3 ml per liter or Carbaryl @ 2 grams per liter after petal fall to kill the young worms before they enter the fruit.

These tiny insects suck sap and produce sticky "honeydew" on the fruit, which turns into black Sooty Mold. The fruit skin may become russeted (rough and brown). Wash the trees with a strong jet of water to remove the sticky honeydew. Spray Imidacloprid @ 0.5 ml per liter or use Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter to control the insects. Controlling the insect stops the black mold problem.
Dark sunken spots develop on fruits causing decay during humid weather. Prune canopy for sunlight and airflow. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during early fruit stage.
Young fruits fall due to moisture stress or nutrient imbalance. Maintain regular irrigation and apply balanced fertilizers. Mulching helps reduce stress.

The base of the fruit or the center heart becomes soft, watery, and smells bad. The fruit rots and pulls out easily. To prevent this, dip the suckers (seeds) in a solution of Mancozeb (2 grams per liter) or Metalaxyl (1 gram per liter) before planting. Improve drainage in the field so water does not stand. If disease appears, spray Fosetyl-Al @ 2 grams per liter on the plants.

The outside of the fruit looks normal, but when you cut it, the eyes inside are black or brown and hard. This is caused by fungi entering through flower parts or mite damage. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during the flowering stage. Since mites help spread this, spray a miticide like Dicofol @ 2 ml per liter if you see insects.

The fruit skin cracks or gets injured, and the inside turns soft, bubbly, and smells like alcohol or vinegar. This happens due to yeast entering wounds. Handle fruits very gently during harvest and transport to avoid cracks. Do not leave harvested fruits in the hot sun; cool them immediately. Dip the cut stem end in a solution of Benomyl or Thiabendazole immediately after harvest.

The side of the fruit facing the sun turns yellow-white or bleached and becomes soft or dried out. The flesh inside loses flavor. Cover the developing fruits with dry grass, straw, or push the plant's own leaves over the fruit to shade it. Planting trees closer together can also provide natural shade for the fruits.

The flesh inside the fruit becomes hard, speckled with brown spots, and very crisp (crunchy). It is a bacterial disease. Clean the harvesting knives with bleach solution frequently to stop spreading it from plant to plant. Control fruit borers and other insects as they carry the bacteria into the fruit. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during fruit development.

Green fruits rotting on the plant, often starting near the soil. This happens in very wet soil. Avoid planting in low-lying areas where water collects. Do not throw soil onto the plant during weeding operations. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter if heavy rains occur while fruits are still green.

The internal flesh becomes hard and corky (leathery) in pockets. This is not a fungus but a reaction to insects or stress. Regular watering is key. Control insects like mites and mealybugs using Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter or appropriate insecticides during the early growth of the fruit to prevent this internal damage.
Maggots feed inside fruits causing sour smell and early drop. Collect fallen fruits and bury them deep. Use bait traps to reduce fruit fly population.
Fruits soften and rot quickly during rainy weather. Remove infected fruits and keep orchard clean. Spray Copper fungicide @ 3 grams per liter during fruit formation.

This is the most damaging disease where the fruit turns soft, watery brown, and gets covered in grey powdery tufts. The fruit rots quickly and often shrivels up (mummies) on the tree. To control this, remove and burn all dried "mummy" fruits remaining on the tree during winter. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Tebuconazole @ 1 ml per liter when the flowers start opening and again 2 weeks before harvest.

The fruit becomes unusually large, puffed up, and hollow like a balloon. It turns pale yellow or grey and eventually dries up and falls. This fungus overwinters on the twigs. Remove and destroy all deformed, puffed-up fruits immediately. The most important treatment is to spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Lime Sulphur just before the buds open in early spring (dormant stage) to kill the fungus before it enters the flower.

Dark, sunken, scabby spots appear on the fruit skin, often causing deep cracks or pits. The fruit may drop early. This disease spreads in warm, wet weather. Avoid planting in low-lying areas with poor air circulation. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter very carefully (as it can burn leaves) or use Agrimycin (Streptocycline) during the petal fall stage. Using resistant varieties is the best long-term solution.

Small, round, olive-green velvety spots appear on the fruit skin. As the fruit grows, these spots turn black and may cause the skin to crack. It usually happens if the orchard is too shady or damp. Prune the tree to allow sunlight to reach the inner branches. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter or Captan @ 2 grams per liter when the fruit shucks (coverings) are splitting off the young fruit.

Pale rings or yellow patterns appear on the fruit skin. The fruit may become deformed, bumpy, and drop prematurely. The flesh inside often has brown streaks. There is no chemical cure for this virus. You must dig out and burn the infected tree immediately to save the rest of the orchard. Control aphids (greenflies) by spraying Dimethoate @ 2 ml per liter, as they spread this virus from tree to tree.

A small beetle cuts a crescent-shaped (half-moon) mark on the fruit skin to lay eggs. The worm eats inside, causing the fruit to rot and drop. Collect and bury all fallen fruits daily to kill the larvae inside. Spray Imidacloprid @ 0.5 ml per liter or Phosmet @ 1.5 grams per liter immediately after the petals fall to kill the adults before they damage the fruit.

This rot attacks ripe fruits during harvest or storage. The fruit turns very soft, leaks liquid, and gets covered in a fluffy white mold with black dots. It enters only through wounds. Handle plums very gently during harvest; do not drop or squeeze them. Cool the fruits immediately after picking. Dip the fruits in a solution of Propiconazole or recommended post-harvest fungicide before packing.

White powdery patches on young fruits eventually disappear, leaving behind hard, brown, rough (rusty) patches on the skin. The fruit does not rot but looks ugly. Prune the tree to reduce humidity. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter or Myclobutanil @ 0.5 ml per liter starting from the petal fall stage to keep the skin smooth.
Ripe berries become soft and covered with grey fuzzy mold, spreading fast in humid weather. Harvest fruits frequently and avoid fruit crowding. Improve air circulation by pruning.

This is the most dangerous disease where oily spots appear on the fruit and later crack open. Immediately cut and burn all infected branches and fruits to stop the spread. After pruning, apply Bordeaux paste on cut ends. Spray a mixture of Streptocycline (0.5 gram) and Copper Oxychloride (2.5 grams) per liter of water. During the rainy season, repeat the spray every 10-15 days and keep the orchard floor very clean.

Small, dark brown spots appear on the fruit skin, which later become hard and sunken. Prune and destroy dried twigs and infected fruits. Spray Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or Propiconazole @ 1 ml per liter during the fruit development stage. If the weather is cloudy and humid, spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter to protect the healthy fruits.

The fruit looks healthy from the outside, but the inside turns black and rotten with a foul smell. This fungus enters through the flower. To prevent this, spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter or Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during the flowering stage. Ensure the tree gets enough Boron and Calcium so the flower end does not crack and let the fungus in.

Fruits crack open, usually due to irregular watering or Boron deficiency. Maintain constant soil moisture by watering regularly; do not let the soil get too dry and then flood it. Spray Borax or Solubor @ 2 grams per liter when the fruits are lemon-sized. Mulching the soil with dry grass helps keep moisture levels steady and prevents cracking.

A black or white hard patch forms on the side of the fruit facing the sun, damaging the quality. Protect the developing fruits by covering them with paper bags or dry grass. Maintain a good leaf canopy by providing balanced nutrition so the leaves naturally shade the fruits. In extreme heat, spray Kaolin clay (50 grams per liter) to create a white protective layer on the fruits.

The butterfly lays eggs on the flower/fruit, and the caterpillar bores inside, causing rot and bad smell. Cover the fruits with butter paper bags or polymer bags when they are the size of a lemon. Remove and destroy any fruits with holes immediately. Spray Neem Oil @ 3 ml per liter or Spinosad @ 0.3 ml per liter when the fruits are small to keep the pest away.

Black necrotic spots cover the fruit surface, reducing its market value. This usually happens in warm, humid weather. Clean the orchard by removing weeds and fallen leaves. Spray Thiophanate Methyl @ 1 gram per liter or Chlorothalonil @ 2 grams per liter. Repeat the spray after 15 days if the spots continue to appear.

Small reddish-brown spots appear, often starting near the crown (calyx) of the fruit, eventually causing rot. Spray Mancozeb @ 2.5 grams per liter or Tebuconazole @ 1 ml per liter during fruit development. Improve air circulation in the orchard by pruning extra branches so humidity does not build up around the fruits.
Fruits split due to irregular watering near maturity. Maintain uniform irrigation and apply mulch. Spray Borax @ 3 grams per liter during fruit growth.
Raised corky lesions appear on fruit surface causing cracking. Prune infected branches and burn them. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during new flush and fruit set.
Maggots develop inside fruits causing foul smell and decay. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury them deep. Use pheromone traps to control fruit flies.
Soft watery rot develops on fruits during humid weather, especially if injured. Avoid injuries during harvest. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter if rot appears.
Maggots feed inside fruits causing sour smell and early drop. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury them deep. Use bait traps to reduce fruit fly population.

Fruits develop soft brown rot during wet weather, especially if injured. Remove infected fruits and improve air circulation by pruning. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during fruit development.

Fruits turn brown and soft with grey fungal growth, especially near maturity. Collect and destroy infected and dried fruits. Prune canopy to allow airflow. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Tebuconazole @ 1 ml per liter during flowering and fruit growth.
Fruit skin splits due to irregular watering near maturity. Maintain uniform soil moisture and avoid drought stress followed by heavy irrigation. Mulching helps prevent cracking.

Dark sunken spots appear on fruit skin, leading to cracking and rot in humid weather. Prune dense canopy and remove infected fruits. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit development.
Fruits split open due to irregular watering and sudden rains. Maintain consistent irrigation and apply mulch around tree base to regulate moisture.
Sunken purple spots appear on berries causing deformation and drying. Remove old canes after harvest and spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during early growth stage.
White powdery coating appears on young fruits, making them rough and misshapen. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter during early fruit stage.
Maggots develop inside fruits causing watery rot and early drop. Collect fallen fruits and bury them deep. Use pheromone traps and bait sprays.
Dark sunken lesions develop on fruit surface causing decay. Prune trees for sunlight and airflow. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during fruit formation.
Birds peck fruits causing wounds that later rot. Use bird nets or reflective ribbons. Harvest fruits early where possible.

This disease causes dark, sunken spots on the fruit, which eventually harden or rot. To control it, prune the tree to remove dead twigs and overcrowded branches. Spray Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter when the fruits are setting. Ensure the orchard is clean and destroy any fallen, rotting fruits immediately to prevent the fungus from spreading to healthy trees.

A black, powdery layer covers the fruit, reducing its market price. This is caused by sticky honeydew from insects like scale insects and mealybugs. To fix this, spray a Starch solution (boil 1 kg Maida in 5 liters of water, cool, and dilute in 20 liters) on the fruits; as it dries, the mold peels off. You must also control the insects by spraying Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter or Dimethoate @ 2 ml per liter.

The branches become flat and twisted, and the fruits produced on them are tiny, clustered, and useless. This is a viral or genetic disorder. The only effective treatment is to cut and remove the flattened branches immediately and apply Bordeaux paste on the cut ends. Do not use grafts or bud sticks from trees that have this problem. Maintain good nutrition to keep the tree strong.

Many young fruits turn yellow and drop off before maturing due to temperature changes or water stress. To stop this, spray NAA (Planofix) @ 4 ml in 18 liters of water twice: once during flowering and again when fruits are pea-sized. Alternatively, spray Gibberellic Acid (GA3) @ 50 ppm. Ensure regular watering during the summer months to keep the soil moisture constant.

The larvae bore into flower buds and young fruits, causing them to dry up and fall with a hole visible. Clean the orchard floor by removing fallen buds and fruits. Install light traps to catch the moths. Spray Quinalphos @ 2 ml per liter or Profenofos @ 1 ml per liter during the bud and flowering stage. Avoid spraying chemicals when the fruit is close to harvest.

This is a serious pest where a tiny worm enters the fruit and eats the seed inside, making the fruit rot from within. The entry hole heals, so the fruit looks fine outside but is bad inside. Collect and burn all fallen fruits. Spray Deltamethrin @ 1 ml per liter or Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter when fruits are marble-sized to prevent the pest from entering.

Small, pinkish to reddish-brown spots appear on the fruit skin, which may join together to form large patches. Prune the canopy to allow sunlight to reach the inner branches. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Thiophanate Methyl @ 1 gram per liter during fruit development. Repeat the spray after 20 days if the weather remains humid.

Caterpillar bores into fruits causing internal rotting and foul smell. Collect and destroy damaged fruits immediately. Spray Neem Oil @ 5 ml per liter or Spinosad @ 0.3 ml per liter during early fruit stage.
Fruits split open due to moisture stress or uneven watering. Maintain regular irrigation and apply mulch to conserve soil moisture. Balanced nutrition helps strengthen fruit skin.

Black sunken lesions develop on fruit surface, leading to rotting and early fruit drop. Prune dense branches and remove infected fruits. Spray Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit setting.

Maggots develop inside fruits causing soft rot and bad smell. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury them deep. Use bait traps or pheromone traps to reduce fruit fly population. Avoid leaving ripe fruits on the tree for long.
Cracks appear on fruit skin due to irregular watering or sudden rain after dry periods. Maintain uniform soil moisture and apply mulch around tree base. Avoid heavy irrigation after drought stress.

Dark sunken spots appear on fruit surface, especially during rainy weather. Prune branches to improve airflow and sunlight. Collect and destroy infected fruits. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit development.

Soft watery rot with green powdery growth appears after harvest through wounds. Harvest carefully without injuries. Dip fruits in hot water (48–50°C for 2–3 minutes) or Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter before storage.

This disease spreads in cool, humid weather and thick crop growth. Keep good air movement by avoiding overcrowding and removing infected fruits and old leaves. Do not irrigate late in the evening. If needed, spray Carbendazim or Hexaconazole @ 1 g per liter of water. Harvest fruits on time and keep them dry during storage to reduce mold development.

This disease occurs when fruits touch wet soil. Use mulching with straw or plastic to keep fruits off the ground. Improve drainage and avoid water stagnation. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb @ 2 g per liter after heavy rains. Remove and destroy infected fruits immediately, as they give bitter taste and spread infection in the field.

Collect and destroy infected fruits regularly to stop spread. Avoid overhead irrigation, especially during flowering and fruiting. Spray Carbendazim or Mancozeb @ 2 g per liter at early fruit stage and repeat if needed. Keep the field clean and rotate crops every season to reduce fungus buildup in soil.

This disease looks like white powder on fruits and leaves and spreads in dry weather. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 g per liter or Hexaconazole @ 1 ml per liter. Remove heavily infected plant parts. Ensure proper spacing between plants for air movement. Balanced fertilizer use helps fruits ripen properly and reduces disease severity.

This disease mainly spreads after harvest through wounds on fruits. Handle fruits carefully during harvesting and transport to avoid injuries. Remove damaged fruits immediately. Keep storage areas clean and dry. Dip harvested fruits in hot water (48–50°C for 2–3 minutes) or spray Carbendazim @ 1 g per liter to reduce rot during storage.

This rot starts near the fruit cap, so always harvest fruits carefully without pulling the green cap. Remove and destroy infected fruits from the field. Avoid overhead watering during fruiting and keep good air circulation. Spray Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl @ 1 g per liter at early fruit stage. Clean field sanitation and timely harvest greatly reduce this disease.

Collect and destroy infected fruits and fallen plant waste regularly. Avoid water splashing on fruits during irrigation. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 g per liter or Chlorothalonil at fruit development stage. Maintain proper plant spacing and apply balanced fertilizer, especially potassium. Good air flow and clean field conditions help prevent further spread and keep fruits market-ready.

This disease spreads during humid weather. Remove affected fruits immediately to stop spread. Avoid dense planting and improve air circulation. Spray Carbendazim or Propiconazole @ 1 g per liter at early symptom stage. Use clean planting material and avoid wetting fruits while watering. Proper drainage and timely spray help fruits remain healthy and smooth.

This rot develops very fast after harvest, especially on injured fruits. Harvest carefully to avoid cuts and bruises. Remove damaged fruits immediately. Keep harvested fruits in a cool, dry place. Dip fruits in hot water at 48–50°C for 2–3 minutes or spray Carbendazim @ 1 g per liter to reduce post-harvest losses.

This disease spreads very fast in hot, humid weather. Remove and destroy infected fruits immediately to stop spread. Avoid overcrowding and ensure good air flow between plants. Do not irrigate late evening. Spray Carbendazim or Mancozeb @ 2 g per liter at early symptoms. Keep the field clean and well-drained to reduce humidity and fungal growth.

Sunscald happens due to strong sunlight, not germs. Protect fruits by maintaining good leaf cover; avoid excessive pruning. Use straw mulch or shade nets to reduce heat stress. Water the field regularly to avoid moisture stress. Balanced fertilizer application helps plants maintain healthy foliage, which naturally shields fruits from direct sun damage.

Collect and destroy mummified fruits from plants and soil, as they spread infection next season. Improve air circulation by proper spacing and pruning. Avoid water splash on fruits. Spray Carbendazim or Propiconazole @ 1 g per liter during flowering and early fruit stage. Good field sanitation is the most effective control method for this disease.

These rots enter through wounds caused by birds, cracks, or rough handling. Control birds using nets and harvest fruits carefully. Remove damaged fruits immediately. Keep storage rooms clean, cool, and dry. Dip fruits in hot water (48–50°C for 2–3 minutes) or spray Carbendazim @ 1 g per liter to reduce post-harvest losses.

The fruit turns brown and soft with grey fungal growth, especially near ripening. Remove mummified fruits from trees and soil. Spray Captan @ 2 grams per liter or Tebuconazole @ 1 ml per liter during flowering and pre-harvest.
Fruits crack open after rain near harvest stage. Maintain balanced irrigation and avoid excess nitrogen. Use rain covers or plastic shelters where possible.
Maggots feed inside fruits making them unfit for consumption. Collect fallen fruits and destroy them. Use sticky traps and spray Spinosad @ 0.3 ml per liter before fruit ripening.
Galls on roots; weak vines; small fruits. Apply Neem cake. Rotate crops.
Fruits split due to irregular watering or Boron deficiency. Maintain uniform irrigation and spray Borax @ 4 grams per liter during fruit development.

Raised corky spots appear on fruit surface reducing market value. Prune infected twigs and destroy affected fruits. Spray Streptocycline (1 g) + Copper Oxychloride (10 g) in 10 liters of water during new flush and fruit set.

Dark brown to black sunken spots appear on pods during humid weather. Prune dense branches to improve air circulation. Collect and destroy infected pods. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during pod development.
White powdery coating appears on flowers and young pods causing poor pod set. Prune overcrowded branches and allow sunlight. Spray Wettable Sulphur @ 2 grams per liter during flowering.

Soft watery rot with green powdery fungus develops after harvest through wounds. Harvest carefully and avoid injuries. Dip fruits in hot water (48–50°C for 2–3 minutes) or Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter before storage.
Fruits split due to irregular watering and moisture stress. Maintain uniform irrigation and apply mulch around tree base. Spray Borax @ 4 grams per liter during fruit development.
Raised corky lesions appear on fruit surface, reducing quality. Prune infected twigs and burn them. Spray Streptocycline + Copper Oxychloride during new flush and early fruit stage.
Dark sunken spots appear on husked fruits in humid weather. Maintain proper spacing for airflow. Remove infected fruits. Spray Copper-based fungicide during fruit development.
Fruits touching wet soil rot quickly. Use mulch or raised beds to keep fruits off the ground. Improve drainage and avoid water stagnation.

This is not a disease. It happens due to lack of calcium and irregular watering. Water the crop regularly and do not allow soil to dry fully or stay flooded. Put mulch like dry leaves or straw to keep moisture. Spray calcium chloride or calcium nitrate on small fruits to help them grow strong and healthy.

This is very common in Karnataka. The worm enters the fruit and eats from inside. Remove and destroy damaged fruits immediately. Use pheromone traps to catch moths early. Grow marigold plants around the field to reduce attack. Spray neem-based spray or biopesticides in the early stage to control worms.

This pest makes tiny holes and damages fruit from inside. Install Tuta pheromone traps and light traps in the field. Remove and burn affected fruits quickly. Do not leave damaged fruits in the field. Rotate crops next season to reduce this pest problem.

Small black or brown sunken spots appear on ripe fruits, especially during rainy weather. Keep fruits off the soil by tying plants to sticks. Harvest fruits as soon as they ripen. Keep the field clean. If rain continues, spray copper-based fungicide to protect fruits.

Dark ring-like spots appear first on old leaves and later on fruits. Remove yellow and infected lower leaves. Give enough space between plants for air movement. Spray Mancozeb or similar fungicide when early symptoms appear on leaves.

Fruits touching wet soil develop round brown spots. Always keep fruits above ground using stakes. Apply straw or plastic mulch to avoid soil contact. Improve drainage and avoid water standing in the field. Raised beds help prevent this problem.

Fruits develop rough brown spots that reduce market value. Avoid sprinkling water on leaves and fruits. Use drip irrigation. Remove affected fruits. Spray copper-based bactericide early to stop further spread during rainy weather.

This virus is common in South India. Infected plants cannot be cured. Remove and destroy the whole plant immediately. Control thrips by fixing blue sticky traps in the field. Spray Neem Oil regularly or Imidacloprid in early stages. Keep the field and borders free from weeds where thrips hide.

This disease appears during cool, cloudy, or misty weather. Spray Mancozeb or Metalaxyl before or at the first sign of disease. Keep enough space between plants so air can flow and leaves dry fast. Avoid watering on leaves, especially in the evening.

Once a plant is infected, it cannot be cured. Remove and destroy infected plants to protect others. Spray copper-based chemicals on healthy plants to reduce spread. Clean knives and tools after use. Always use certified disease-free seeds for the next crop.

This is sunburn, not a disease. It happens in hot weather when fruits are exposed to direct sunlight. Do not remove too many leaves. Allow leaves to shade fruits naturally. During extreme heat, use a light shade net (30%) to protect fruits.

This happens due to sudden heavy watering after dry conditions. Water the crop regularly and evenly. Use mulch to maintain soil moisture. Avoid excess irrigation after rain. Choose crack-resistant varieties if possible. Remove cracked fruits early to avoid rotting.

Fruits become misshapen and scarred, especially in cold North Indian winters. This is not a disease. Avoid planting sensitive varieties during very cold months. Do not apply excess nitrogen fertilizer. Proper planting time is the best solution; sprays will not help.

Fruits look normal but feel light and empty inside. This happens due to poor pollination during very hot or very cold weather. Gently shake plants during daytime to help pollen movement. Avoid spraying chemicals during flowering as they reduce bee activity.
Yellow patches on top; purple fuzz underneath. Treatment: Keep leaves dry. Prune for airflow. Use resistant varieties like "Prospera."

Small white rings appear on fruits in cool and damp weather. Reduce humidity by removing excess leaves so air can pass through plants. In protected cultivation, keep good ventilation. Remove affected fruits. Spray Chlorothalonil only if wet weather continues.

Ripe fruits develop black powdery mold, mainly after rain near harvest. Harvest fruits as soon as they ripen. Avoid fruit cracking and sunburn. Handle fruits carefully during picking so the skin is not damaged.

White or yellow cloudy patches appear on fruit skin, and taste becomes poor. This is caused by stink bugs sucking fruit juice. Keep the field and borders free of weeds. Handpick bugs using gloves. Spray Neem Oil to stop bugs from feeding.
Maggots feed inside fruit causing soft rot and bad smell. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury them deep. Use bait traps and avoid leaving ripe fruits on plants.
Sunken dark spots develop on fruit skin leading to rot. Prune plants to improve airflow. Remove infected fruits. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit growth.
Soft watery rot with green powdery fungus develops after harvest through wounds. Harvest carefully and avoid injuries. Dip fruits in hot water (48–50°C for 2–3 minutes) before storage.
Fruit skin splits due to irregular watering or moisture stress. Maintain uniform irrigation and apply mulch to regulate soil moisture.

Raised corky lesions appear on fruit surface reducing market value. Prune infected twigs and destroy affected fruits. Spray Streptocycline (1 g) + Copper Oxychloride (10 g) in 10 liters of water during new flush.
Dark sunken spots appear on berries causing shrinkage and rot. Remove infected fruits and fallen debris. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during fruit development.

Ripe berries become soft and covered with grey fuzzy mold during cool, humid weather. Harvest fruits frequently and do not allow over-ripening. Prune bushes to improve air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation during fruiting.
Maggots feed inside fruits causing sour smell and early drop. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury them deep. Use bait traps to reduce fruit fly population.
Fruits develop soft brown rot during rainy season. Collect and destroy infected fruits immediately. Improve drainage and airflow by pruning. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit growth.

Pods develop soft brown rot, often starting near the tip or stalk, especially under high humidity. Improve drainage and avoid water stagnation. Remove and destroy infected pods immediately. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during pod development.

Dark sunken spots appear on pods, causing shriveling and poor quality. Maintain proper shade and air circulation. Prune excess vines. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter or Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter during early pod stage.
Maggots develop inside fruits causing foul smell and early fruit drop. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury them deep. Use bait traps to reduce fruit fly population.

Fruits soften and rot during rainy weather, especially if damaged. Collect fallen fruits and maintain orchard hygiene. Improve air flow by pruning. Spray Copper fungicide @ 3 grams per liter during fruit growth.
Fruit skin splits due to moisture stress and irregular watering. Maintain uniform irrigation and apply mulch to conserve soil moisture.
Small dark sunken spots appear on fruit skin leading to cracking and rot. Prune branches to improve sunlight. Remove infected fruits. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter during fruit development.

This is the most dangerous disease. Small, water-soaked spots appear on the green husk, which quickly turn black and sunken. The nut inside shrivels, turns black, and rots. To control it, spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter or Bordeaux Mixture (1%) starting when the female flowers (catkins) appear. Repeat the spray every 7-10 days if the weather is wet during spring. Avoid overhead sprinklers as water splashing spreads the bacteria.

Circular, sunken, brown spots appear on the green husk. If the infection is severe, the nut drops early or the kernel inside shrivels. The shell may get stained dark. Clean the orchard by burning fallen leaves and nuts in winter, as the fungus lives there. Spray Mancozeb @ 2.5 grams per liter or Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter when the leaves are unfolding and again when the nuts are small.

White or bleached patches appear on the fruit surface exposed to strong sunlight. Maintain good leaf cover to shade fruits. Avoid heavy pruning. Use straw or plant leaves to cover exposed fruits during peak summer.

The larva (worm) bores into the young nut through the blossom end, eating the kernel inside. You will see black waste (frass) at the entry hole. The damaged nuts fall early. Use pheromone traps to catch male moths. Spray Spinosad @ 0.3 ml per liter or Carbaryl @ 2 grams per liter when the moths are flying (usually late spring). Remove and destroy all fallen, infested nuts immediately.

Maggots feed inside the green husk, turning it into a black, soft, mushy liquid. This stains the nut shell a dirty black color and makes the kernel shrivel. Hang yellow sticky traps to catch the flies. Spray a bait mixture (Jaggery/Molasses + Malathion) on the leaves to attract and kill the flies before they lay eggs. This does not damage the nut directly but ruins the quality and price.

The nut looks fine outside, but when cracked, the kernel is covered in green, blue, or black mold. This happens if the hull splits but the nut is not harvested quickly, or if insects damage the shell. Harvest the nuts as soon as 80% of the hulls have split; do not leave them on the tree. Dry the harvested nuts immediately to remove moisture. Controlling sunburn and insect damage also prevents mold.

The side of the green husk facing the hot sun turns yellow or brown and becomes hard. The kernel inside may darken or shrivel. This happens in peak summer. Maintain a healthy canopy of leaves to shade the nuts by providing enough water and fertilizer. In extreme heat, you can whitewash the tree trunks or use overhead misters to cool the orchard, but avoid keeping the nuts wet for too long.

While this affects branches, the main symptom farmers see is the husk and nut drying up suddenly and sticking to the branch (mummies). The outer husk turns greyish-brown. Prune the affected branch well below the wilted part and burn it. Do not shake the tree when harvesting infected nuts, as this spreads fungal spores. Maintain tree health with proper irrigation.

Sunken, circular spots appear on the fruit rind, which turn black during rain, causing the fruit to crack or rot. Clean the field by destroying infected vines and fruits and do not plant watermelon in the same place every year. Spray Carbendazim @ 1 gram per liter or Mancozeb @ 2.5 grams per liter when fruits start forming. Handle fruits carefully to avoid skin damage during harvest.

Dark, water-soaked, oily stains appear on the top surface of the fruit, eventually causing the skin to crack and the fruit to rot inside. This spreads fast in warm, wet weather. Use only certified disease-free seeds. If you see symptoms, spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter mixed with Streptocycline (small packet) immediately. Avoid overhead watering (sprinklers) as it splashes bacteria onto the fruit.

The bottom end of the fruit (where the flower was) turns black, leathery, and flat. This is not a fungus but a result of Calcium deficiency and irregular watering. Maintain steady soil moisture by watering regularly; do not let the soil get too dry and then flood it. Spray Calcium Chloride or Calcium Nitrate @ 2 grams per liter when fruits are small (marble-sized) to fix the deficiency.

The part of the fruit touching the wet soil turns brown, soft, and develops mold. To prevent this, do not let fruits sit directly on the soil. Place a piece of wood, stone, or a bed of dry straw (mulch) under each fruit. You can also use plastic mulch sheets before planting. Spraying the soil under the vines with Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter can help reduce the fungus.

Large white or bleached patches appear on the fruit surface exposed to direct sunlight, making the area weak and prone to rot. Maintain a healthy leaf canopy to shade the fruits by providing proper fertilizers. Cover exposed fruits with dry straw, newspaper caps, or the plant's own leaves during the peak summer heat to protect the skin.

While this attacks stems, it also causes black, wrinkled rot on the fruit, often with gummy oozing. It usually enters through wounds. Clean up crop debris after harvest. Spray Chlorothalonil @ 2 grams per liter or Mancozeb @ 2.5 grams per liter. Ensure good air circulation in the field and avoid injuring the fruit during weeding or turning.

The fruit becomes bumpy, mottled (mixed colors), and deformed, making it hard to sell. This is spread by aphids (greenflies). Remove and destroy weeds around the field where aphids hide. Pull out and bury infected plants immediately. Spray Imidacloprid @ 0.5 ml per liter or Dimethoate @ 2 ml per liter to control the aphids and stop the spread.

The fruit develops soft spots that may turn into white or pink moldy patches, often starting at the stem end. Use resistant varieties if available. Dip the fruit in hot water (55°C) for 2 minutes after harvest to clean the skin. Avoid pulling the fruit from the vine; always cut it with a clipper to leave a smooth stem, preventing the fungus from entering.

Water-soaked soft rot develops on fruits touching wet soil, especially during rainy weather. Use plastic mulch or dry straw to keep fruits off the ground. Improve field drainage. Spray Metalaxyl + Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter if heavy rains occur.

Dark sunken circular spots appear on fruit skin, later causing cracking and rot. Remove infected fruits and vines. Avoid overhead irrigation. Spray Mancozeb @ 2 grams per liter or Chlorothalonil @ 2 grams per liter during fruit development.
Seedlings topple and rot at soil line. Treatment: Avoid over-seeding. Use sterilized potting mix. Ensure excellent ventilation.

Maggots develop inside fruits causing foul smell and early drop. Collect fallen fruits daily and bury them deep. Use bait traps to reduce fruit fly population. Avoid leaving ripe fruits on the tree for long periods.

Fruits soften and rot during humid weather, especially if injured. Collect and destroy fallen fruits. Prune branches to improve airflow. Spray Copper Oxychloride @ 3 grams per liter during fruit growth stage.

Fruits develop brown-black rot under prolonged moisture and poor air movement. Remove infected fruits and improve ventilation. Avoid water stagnation around trees. Copper-based fungicide spray helps reduce spread.

Brown or reddish pustules appear on the undersides of leaves. Treatment: Agathi leaves are often eaten as greens or fodder. Avoid systemic fungicides. Prune the infected branches. Spray diluted Sulphur or Neem oil. Ensure the tree gets full sun.

Green caterpillars eat the leaves and tunnel into the flower buds, ruining the edible flowers. Treatment: Since the flowers are eaten directly, avoid harsh chemicals. Handpick the caterpillars. Shake the tree gently to drop them. Spray a diluted Neem oil solution (2ml per liter) if the infestation is severe.
Larvae bore into the stem, causing wilting. Treatment: Inject neem oil into the bore hole and seal with clay.

Caterpillars spin webs around the leaves and flowers (the edible part) and eat them from inside. Treatment: Since flowers are delicate, handpick the caterpillars or shake the tree gently to dislodge them. Spray a dilute neem oil solution. Encourage birds in the garden.

A white powdery coating appears on the leaves and pods, causing them to dry up and drop early. This is common in dry, cool weather. Prune the tree to improve sunlight penetration. Spray wettable sulfur (2g/liter) or a biological control like Ampelomyces quisqualis. If harvesting for food, a baking soda spray (1 tsp + 1 liter water) is a safe, non-toxic alternative.

Brown or black circular spots appear on the edible leaves, rendering them unappealing. Remove heavily infected leaves to stop the spread. Improve air circulation by thinning branches. If severe, spray a copper-based fungicide, but observe a strict waiting period (7-10 days) before harvesting leaves for consumption. Avoid overhead watering in the evening.

Larvae bore into the long pods and eat the developing seeds. Look for small holes and frass. Manually remove infested pods. Install light traps to catch adult moths. Spray Neem oil or Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) during the flowering and pod-formation stage. Regular harvesting of mature pods prevents the population from building up.

Though primarily in the stem, severe infestation cuts off nutrients, causing the edible leaves and flowers to wilt and yellow. Look for sawdust at the base. Inject a Neem oil solution into the bore holes and seal with clay. Maintain tree vigor with organic compost; healthy trees resist borers better.

Leaves show mottled yellow and green patterns and may become deformed. There is no cure. Remove and burn the infected branches or the whole tree if young. Control aphids and whiteflies which spread the virus using sticky traps or insecticidal soap.

The larvae weave the tender leaves and flower buds together with silk and feed from inside. Since Agathi leaves are often eaten raw or lightly cooked, avoid harsh chemicals. Handpick the webbed clusters and destroy them. Spray an aqueous extract of Neem kernel or a simple soap solution. Encourage birds in the garden as they naturally predate on these caterpillars.

Small brown spots or rusty pustules appear on the leaves. Treatment: This vine is very hardy and semi-wild. Usually requires no treatment, but if severe, remove the infected leaves to keep the vine healthy. Ensure it has a strong tree or trellis to climb into the sunlight.

This appears as brown, dry, and powdery internal rot in stored bulbils. Prevention is your best defense: always "cure" your harvest by letting bulbils dry in a shaded, airy spot for several days before long-term storage to toughen the skin. Avoid bruising them during handling. If you find a small infected spot, cut it out and coat the wound with clean wood ash or lime to seal it. Discard completely hollow or light-weight bulbils.

This causes the edible bulbils to become mushy, wet, and foul-smelling. To treat, you must remove and destroy infected bulbils immediately to stop the "ooze" from infecting healthy ones. Keep your storage area cool, dry, and well-ventilated. Avoid washing the bulbils with water before storage; instead, gently brush off the dirt. Sanitize any knife used on infected parts with a bleach solution before touching healthy potatoes.

These microscopic pests cause cracking and dark, flaky rot just beneath the skin of the tuber. Since they persist in the soil and seed, always use certified clean bulbils for planting. If you suspect your soil is infected, practice crop rotation and do not plant yams there for 3 years. For harvest protection, a hot water treatment (soaking tubers in 50°C water for 30 minutes) can kill the nematodes without harming the potato.

Often seen as a bluish-green fuzzy growth on stored potatoes, this fungus attacks through cuts and scrapes. Handle your harvest gently to prevent skin injuries. Reduce humidity in your storage room to starve the fungus. If infection is surface-level, you can wipe it off with a cloth dipped in vinegar. Check your stored supply weekly and isolate any moldy bulbils instantly to prevent the spores from drifting onto the rest of your stock.

The stem swells at certain points. The plant growth is stunted and it may break easily. Larvae are tunneling inside. Treatment: This is a major pest for Amaranth. Pull out and destroy infected plants. Harvest the greens early before the population builds up. Clean cultivation (remove weeds) is essential.

White blisters appear on the underside of leaves. The upper side shows yellow patches. Treatment: Avoid overhead watering. Harvest frequently to remove the inoculum. If severe, spray a mild copper fungicide, but wait 7-10 days before harvesting greens for food.

White, raised blisters appear on the undersides of leaves, while the upper side shows yellow patches. This ruins the leafy green quality. Harvest early if spots appear. Rotate crops; do not plant amaranth in the same spot repeatedly. Spray Mancozeb or Ridomil if not harvesting immediately, but stick to safety periods.

Leaves develop brown, water-soaked spots that rot rapidly, especially during rainy seasons (wet rot). Improve drainage and avoid dense planting. Remove infected plants immediately. Spraying with cow urine (diluted 1:10) or Neem oil can act as a preventive bio-fungicide.

Grubs bore into the succulent edible stems, causing the plant to wither and break. Look for swellings on the stem. Cut open swollen stems to kill larvae. Remove wild amaranth weeds nearby which host the pest. Soil application of Neem cake helps repel the adults from laying eggs.

Caterpillars roll leaves together and feed inside. Hand squeezing the rolled leaves kills the larvae (if you are not squeamish) or pick them off. Spraying a 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) is very effective and safe for leafy greens.

Affects young seedlings/microgreens; the stem rots at the soil line and the plant topples. Use sterilized potting soil. Do not overwater. Treat seeds with Trichoderma viride before sowing. Ensure plenty of sunlight and air circulation for seedlings.

Clusters of green/black insects on the stem and leaf undersides suck sap and cause curling. Wash with a strong jet of water. Spray soapy water or Neem oil. Ladybugs are excellent natural controllers for this pest.
Yellow veins and mottled leaves. The leaves become small and brittle. Pull out infected plants immediately. Control the vectors (aphids/whiteflies). Keep the field weed-free.

A specific beetle (Podontia) eats the leaves, sometimes stripping the tree bare (defoliation). Treatment: Look for large, colorful beetles on the leaves in June-July. Handpick them (they are sluggish in the morning). Dig up the soil around the tree base in summer to kill the pupae hiding there.

Maggots bore into the mature green fruit, causing it to rot from the inside and fall prematurely. Treatment: This is the biggest problem for Amatekayi. Hang "Methyl Eugenol" traps on the tree branches when fruits start developing. Collect and bury fallen fruits deep in the ground to break the cycle.

Black, sunken spots appear on the fruit skin, which may lead to rotting. Prune the tree to allow light to the inner branches. Spray Copper Oxychloride before flowering and after fruit set. Post-harvest, wash fruits in warm water (50°C) to reduce surface infection.
Tiny insects cause upward curling of leaves and scabby/corky streaks on the fruit skin. Use blue sticky traps. Spray Imidacloprid or Neem oil.

A black, sticky coating covers the fruit and leaves, growing on honeydew from scale insects. It makes the fruit look dirty. Control the scale insects with Neem oil. Wash the harvested fruit with a mild soap solution to remove the mold before selling or eating.

Corky, brown, raised lesions appear on the fruit surface. It is difficult to cure. Prune infected twigs during the dry season. Spray Streptocycline (an antibiotic) coupled with copper fungicide during early fruit development.
Rot starts at the stalk end of the harvested fruit and spreads downwards. Avoid pulling fruits; clip them with a stalk attached. Prevent bruising during harvest. Store in a cool, dry place.
Small, waxy bumps on the fruit surface suck sap and ruin the appearance. Scrub them off with a soft brush if the infestation is light. Prune heavily infested branches. Apply horticultural oil spray.
Fuzzy gray mold on lower leaves touching soil. Treatment: Mulch to keep leaves off mud. Water in the morning.
Young fruits drop off due to water stress or nutrient lack. Mulch the tree base to retain moisture. Water regularly during fruit setting. Apply a balanced fertilizer with micronutrients.

Maggots feed inside the ripening fruit, causing it to rot and drop. Set up methyl eugenol pheromone traps to catch male flies. Collect and bury all fallen fruits to break the cycle. Harvest fruits while they are mature but still firm (green) to avoid infestation.

Coastal/Kerala Crop. Large, irregular brown spots with yellow halos appear on the leaves. Leaves dry up, reducing tuber yield. Treatment: Cut off and burn infected leaves. Ensure the soil drains well, as high humidity fuels the fungus. Mulch with dry leaves to prevent soil splash.

This causes the rhizomes to turn soft, watery, and mushy with a distinct foul odor. It thrives in wet, poorly drained soils. To manage it, immediately dig up and destroy any infected plants to prevent the bacteria from spreading to the soil. Ensure you plant in raised beds with excellent drainage. After harvest, wash the rhizomes in clean water and let them dry completely in a cool area before storage. discard any tubers with cuts or bruises immediately.

This infection creates water-soaked lesions on the rhizomes that eventually turn brown and decay, especially in waterlogged conditions. Prevention is key: never overwater your crop and ensure the soil is loose and sandy. If you detect rot during the growing season, reduce watering immediately and improve airflow. When planting next season, treat your seed rhizomes with a biological fungicide like Trichoderma to protect them from soil-borne spores. Rotate crops and avoid planting in the same spot for 3 years.

Unlike soft rot, this fungus causes the internal flesh of the arrowroot to become dry, powdery, and brown while the skin wrinkles. It often enters through harvest wounds. To treat, you must "cure" your harvest by leaving the rhizomes in a warm, shaded, well-ventilated spot for a few days to heal minor skin injuries. Handle the harvest gently to avoid bruises. If you see white or pink mold developing on stored tubers, remove them instantly to save the rest.

disease_name: Banded Leaf and Sheath Blight (Fungal Infection)
treatment: While often seen on leaves, this fungus (Rhizoctonia solani) can travel down and rot the rhizome scales, causing brown, scabby lesions. It spreads rapidly in hot, humid weather. To control it, strip away infected lower leaves and keep the base of the plant clear of weeds and debris. Avoid piling soil too high against the stems. If the infection is severe, harvest the mature rhizomes early to prevent the rot from penetrating deeper into the edible flesh.

These microscopic worms burrow into the rhizome, causing dark, necrotic tunnels inside the white flesh, which leads to secondary rotting. Since they live in the soil, your best treatment is hot water disinfection: soak your planting material in 50°C water for 20–30 minutes before planting. Add plenty of organic compost or neem cake to your soil, as this encourages beneficial microbes that naturally suppress nematode populations. Avoid planting arrowroot in soil previously used for bananas or ginger.
Fuzzy gray mold appears on the flower head. Treatment: Ensure wide spacing. Avoid overhead watering. Harvest early in damp weather.
Tiny black beetles chew "shotholes" in leaves. Treatment: Use yellow sticky traps. Cover young plants with fine mesh. Dust leaves with wood ash.

This is the most destructive pest. Adult flies puncture young fruits to lay eggs, and maggots eat the inside, causing the fruit to rot. Treatment: Wrap young fruits in newspaper or cloth bags as soon as they set (finger size) to create a physical barrier. Use "Methyl Eugenol" pheromone traps to lure and catch male flies. Collect and bury any fallen, infested fruit deep in the soil to kill the maggots.

Water-soaked, soft lesions appear on the fruit, usually where it touches damp soil. White cottony fungus may grow on the spot. Treatment: Prevention is the only real cure. Never let the gourd sit on bare soil; place a wooden board, stone, or thick straw mulch under every fruit. Improve soil drainage and avoid watering in the late evening. If infection starts, harvest immediately and cut away the rotting part.

Young fruits turn black and shrivel starting from the blossom end (tip), often dropping off. Treatment: This is often due to poor pollination or calcium deficiency. Hand-pollinate female flowers in the morning to ensure fruit set. Keep soil moisture consistent (not soaked) to help the roots absorb calcium. Add lime or crushed eggshells to the soil to boost calcium levels. Remove rotting young fruits immediately.

While this affects the whole plant, it specifically causes the fruit to become small, deformed, and "warty" (bumpy), making it unappealing. Treatment: There is no cure. Remove and burn the infected plant immediately to save the rest. The virus is spread by aphids, so control them using yellow sticky traps or insecticidal soap sprays. Sterilize pruning tools with alcohol after touching an infected plant.
Yellow spots on top of leaves, grey fuzz below. Leaves dry up. Treatment: Trellis the vines to keep them off damp soil. Prune dense foliage. Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens (bio-agent).

Maggots bore into the developing gourd, causing soft rot and premature yellowing. Wrap individual fruits in newspaper or cloth bags when they are small. Use pheromone traps. Destroy all damaged fruits.
White powder on leaves and stems reduces plant energy, leading to small, poor-quality fruits. Spray wettable sulfur or Karathane. Remove weed hosts. Ensure vines are well-spaced.
Yellow angular spots on leaves that turn brown; it can affect fruit quality. Spray Mancozeb or Metalaxyl. Avoid overhead watering. Prune lower leaves to increase airflow near the soil.
Fruits become bumpy, small, and mottled green/yellow. Leaves curl. Remove infected plants immediately. Control aphids and whiteflies. Use virus-resistant varieties if available.
Orange beetles eat holes in flowers and young fruit skin. Handpick beetles in the early morning when they are sluggish. Dust wood ash on the plants. Spray Neem oil to repel them.
Causes gummy ooze on stems and black rot on the fruit. Rotate crops (don't plant gourds for 2-3 years). Use treated seeds. Spray Chlorothalonil if symptoms appear.

The bottom end of the fruit turns black and leathery. This is not a germ but a calcium lack often caused by irregular watering. Water consistently. Mulch the soil. Add lime or gypsum to the soil before planting.
Blue-black beetles eat spear tips. Treatment: Handpick beetles. Cut and burn old ferns in autumn to remove hiding spots.

Almost every wild fig is infested with tiny wasps/flies. The fruit looks ripe but is full of insects inside. Treatment: For culinary use (cooking raw figs), harvest them when they are still firm and green (unripe). Cut them open and soak in salted turmeric water for 30 minutes to drive out any insects. Use pheromone traps in the garden.

The undersides of leaves are covered in rusty brown dust. Leaves fall off early. Treatment: This usually affects the tree after the rains. Rake up and burn the fallen leaves. Prune the tree to improve airflow. It usually recovers on its own without chemical treatment.

This is the most common issue where larvae bore into the fruit, making it inedible and filled with frass. Collect and destroy all fallen, infested fruits immediately to break the breeding cycle. You can protect the fruit clusters by bagging them with fine mesh or cloth bags when they are small to physically prevent moths from laying eggs. Applying neem oil spray early in the fruit-setting stage helps repel the adult moths effectively.

Symptoms include dark, sunken, circular spots on the fig skin which can turn pinkish during wet weather. Prune the tree to open up the canopy, allowing sunlight to dry the fruits quickly after rain. Remove and burn any dried, mummified fruits left on the tree from the previous season. If severe, spray a copper-based fungicide or Bordeaux mixture during the early fruit formation stage. Avoid overhead irrigation to keep the fruit surface dry.

Sudden heavy watering after a dry spell causes the skin to split, allowing yeast and bacteria to enter and cause sour fermentation. Prevention is entirely about water management; keep the soil moisture consistent by mulching the base of the tree with organic matter. Harvest split fruits immediately if they aren't rotten yet. If they smell sour or attract fruit flies, dispose of them far away to prevent the spread of souring bacteria to healthy figs.

While primarily on leaves, severe rust causes rusty-brown pustules on the fruit skin, making them rough and unappealing. Clean up all fallen leaves and debris around the tree base to remove overwintering spores. Avoid wetting the fruit clusters when watering. Thinning the fruit clusters can help improve airflow around individual figs. If necessary, use a sulfur-based organic fungicide, but ensure it is safe for edible fruits and apply it well before harvest time.

This fungus can attack ripening figs, causing them to turn brown, mushy, and covered in gray mold. It usually strikes during cool, damp weather. Promptly harvest ripe fruit; do not let over-ripe figs hang on the tree. Prune dense branches to increase air circulation, which helps the fruit dry out. If you spot a moldy fig, remove it gently without shaking it to avoid releasing spores onto adjacent healthy fruits.

The plant looks bushy at the top (like a broom) and leaves have yellow/white streaks. It fails to produce cobs. Treatment: Use resistant hybrid seeds. There is no cure for the infected plant; pull it out and burn it. Drain the field well, as waterlogging encourages this fungus.

You will see "shot holes" (pinholes) in the leaves as they unfurl. The central shoot may die. Treatment: Since Baby Corn is harvested very young (within 50-60 days), chemical sprays are risky. Apply a pinch of ash or sand mixed with lime into the central plant funnel to irritate and drive out the larvae.
Larvae feed on the silk and the tip of the young cob. Apply Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or Spinosad to the silks. Mineral oil applied to the silk channel can suffocate larvae.
Large, grey, puffball-like galls form on the kernels. Remove galls immediately before they burst and release spores. Avoid mechanical injury to plants. distinct varieties are more resistant.
White or pinkish mold on the kernels; kernels may rot. Plant resistant hybrids. Balance nitrogen fertilizers. Harvest baby corn early before the fungus can establish in the ear.
Large, boat-shaped grey lesions on leaves reduce photosynthesis, leading to small, poorly filled ears. Spray Mancozeb or Zineb. Rotate crops with non-grass species.
Brown pustules on husks and leaves make the ear unappealing. Plant resistant varieties. Spray wettable sulfur if infection is early. destroy crop debris after harvest.

The stalk and ear shank turn soft, slimy, and smell of rotting fish. The ear may drop. Avoid waterlogging. Use chlorinated water for irrigation if possible. Bleaching powder drenching (light) can help soil sanitation.
Swarms of aphids inside the husk make the baby corn sticky and sooty. Spray Neem oil or soap solution. Encourage ladybugs. Check husks carefully before marketing.

The tender emerging shoot turns brown, soft, and rots before it grows tall. This often happens in waterlogged clumps. Treatment: Keep the bamboo clump clean; remove old, dead stems to improve airflow. Ensure water doesn't stagnate around the base. Cover the emerging shoot with a mound of dry soil to protect it from direct moisture and harvest it quickly while tender.

Larvae bore into the soft, young shoot, causing the tip to dry up ("dead heart") and the shoot to die. Treatment: This is common in the forest areas of Malnad. Clear away fallen leaves around the clump to remove hiding spots. If you see a bore hole, the shoot is likely spoiled; remove it. Light traps during the monsoon season help catch the adult moths.

This infection attacks young, tender shoots just as they emerge, causing water-soaked brown lesions that eventually turn the whole shoot into a soft, rotting mass smelling of molasses. To save your crop, ensure excellent soil drainage and remove any rotting debris from the clump base before the rainy season. If infection spots appear, drench the soil with a copper-based fungicide or use Trichoderma bio-agents. Harvest healthy shoots early to minimize exposure to wet soil conditions.

This virus creates hard, brown, necrotic streaks inside the white flesh of the shoot (often called "nails"), ruining its texture and market value. Since there is no chemical cure, your primary tool is sterilization. The virus spreads mainly through infected harvesting knives; always dip your tools in a bleach solution or heat them between cuts. Dig up and burn infected clumps to stop the spread. Always source certified virus-free seedlings for new plantations.

This causes the harvested shoots to become mushy, slimy, and foul-smelling, especially at the cut end. It enters through harvest wounds. Prevent this by harvesting carefully to avoid splitting the base. Keep harvested shoots dry and cool; never wash them in dirty water. If you must store them, trim the cut end cleanly and coat it with a lime paste or food-grade wax to seal out bacteria. Process or cook the shoots immediately after harvest if possible.

Larvae bore deep into the tender shoot, creating tunnels filled with excrement and causing the shoot to rot from the inside. Watch for small entry holes or wilting tips on young shoots. Remove and destroy infested shoots immediately to kill the larvae before they mature. Light traps can catch adult moths at night. For organic control, apply neem oil to the soil and base of the clump during the emergence season to repel the pests from laying eggs.
Tiny leaves; bushy plant; no fruit. Remove plant. Control leafhoppers.

This fungus attacks the connection point between the rhizome and the shoot, causing the shoot to discolor and die before it fully emerges. It is often linked to waterlogging. Improve aeration by thinning out old, crowded culms from the center of the clump. Apply a soil drench of Bordeaux mixture (copper sulfate and lime) around the clump base. Avoid piling wet soil or compost directly against the emerging shoots during the wettest months.
Small waxy bumps on shoots causing stunted growth. Treatment: Scrub off scales with a soft brush. Apply Neem oil spray. Ensure the bamboo clump is thinned for light.

Very Common. Small yellow spots on leaves turn into brown streaks. Leaves die early, leaving the bunch without food. Treatment: Cut off infected leaves and leave them on the ground (face down). Ensure good drainage. A spray of mineral oil or neem-based fungicides helps protect remaining green leaves.

The plant topples over easily. The underground rhizome is soft and rotting with a foul smell. Treatment: Use healthy suckers. Dip suckers in copper oxychloride solution before planting. Ensure excellent drainage.

The lower leaves turn bright yellow and hang down around the stem like a skirt. The plant eventually dies. Treatment: This fungus lives in the soil for years. There is no cure for the infected plant; dig it out and burn it. Do not replant banana in that spot. Use resistant varieties (like "Nendran" or "Poovan").
The tip of the fruit dries out and looks like the ash of a cigar. Remove the flower remnants (pistils) from the finger tips in the field as soon as fruit forms. Bag the bunches.

The cut surface of the "hand" (where it joins the stalk) turns black and rots, causing fingers to drop. Clean cutting knives. Treat the cut crown with alum or fungicide paste immediately after de-handing.
Grubs bore into the corm and stem, but can also attack fruit stalks, leading to small bunches. Use clean planting material (corms). Trapping with cut stem pieces works well. Apply Neem cake to soil.
Plants are stunted; bunches are small and deformed. Leaves bunch at the top. Dig up and destroy infected mats immediately. Control aphids which spread the virus. Use virus-free tissue culture plants.

Beetles feed on the skin of young fruit, leaving rough, scabby scars that ruin market value. Bag the bunch with plastic or cloth covers immediately after the hands open. Keep the plantation weed-free.
Sandpaper-like raised black spots on the fruit peel and leaves. Bagging bunches helps. Prune infected leaves. Spray Mancozeb or mineral oil during fruit development.
Dark, sunken spots on the ripe fruit peel; the flesh inside may rot. Wash fruit after harvest to remove latex. Dip in hot water (50°C for 5 mins) or fungicide before storage. Avoid bruising.

New leaves are narrow, upright, and bunched together at the top (like a brush). The plant stops growing and won't produce the flower/fruit. Treatment: This is a serious virus spread by aphids. There is no cure. Inject the infected plant with herbicide or dig it out completely and burn it. Do not plant new suckers near infected areas. Control aphids to prevent spread.

Small yellow spots on leaves turn into brown streaks. Leaves die early, leaving the bunch (and flower) without food. Treatment: Cut off the infected leaves and leave them on the ground (face down). Ensure good drainage in the plantation. A spray of mineral oil or neem-based fungicides helps protect the remaining green leaves.

This infection turns the flower tip and bracts soft, mushy, and foul-smelling, often spreading from the fruit tip upwards. It thrives in hot, wet weather. To stop it, cut off the infected flower bell immediately using a sterilized knife to save the rest of the bunch. disposing of the rotting material far from the plant is crucial. Ensure good airflow around the bunch by removing excess leaves. disinfect tools with bleach between cuts to prevent spreading the bacteria.

You will see black, sunken, or necrotic spots on the outer purple bracts of the flower, which can penetrate the inner florets. To manage this, remove and discard the damaged outer layers before bringing them into the kitchen. On the plant, ensure the flower does not rub against leaves or stems, as injuries invite fungus. In severe cases, bag the developing bunch with a perforated plastic sleeve to keep it dry and protected from spores and pests.

Thrips are tiny insects that hide inside the tight bracts, causing rusty, brown, and corky streaks on the flower petals and florets. While often cosmetic on the outer layers, heavy infestation can ruin the texture. Prevention involves bagging the flower early in its development. For harvested flowers, soak the blossom in salt water or turmeric water for 20 minutes before cooking; this drives the insects out and cleans the florets effectively. Neem oil spray on the plant also helps.

This fungus causes the tip of the flower (and emerging fingers) to dry out, turn grey/black, and look like burnt ash or a cigar tip. It enters through the dying florets. To treat, manually remove the pistils and withered floral parts as soon as the hands form. If the flower bell itself is infected, harvest it immediately. Improve field sanitation by removing trash from around the mat, as the fungus survives in decaying plant debris.

Aphids cluster under the bracts, sucking sap and leaving sticky honeydew that attracts black sooty mold, making the flower unappealing. They also transmit the Bunchy Top Virus. Control them by spraying a strong jet of water or insecticidal soap directly into the bract crevices. If harvesting for food, discard the outer layers and wash the inner heart thoroughly in vinegar water. Introducing beneficial insects like lady beetles into your garden can naturally keep the aphid population down.
Plants yellow and die; roots rot. Use wilt-resistant varieties. Rotate crops for 5 years.

The pods develop small water-soaked spots that turn brown and sunken, rendering them inedible. Treatment: Use seeds from healthy plants only. Remove infected plants immediately to prevent spreading bacteria. Avoid overhead sprinklers; always water at the base to keep pods dry. A preventative spray of a copper-based fungicide can help protect the remaining healthy pods if the weather is humid.

Caterpillars bore holes into the green pods and eat the developing seeds inside. Treatment: Handpick and destroy any visible caterpillars. Remove any pods with holes instantly. Use pheromone traps to catch adult moths. Spraying a 5% Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE) when flowering starts helps deter the moths from laying eggs on the young pods.

Dark, sunken, circular spots with reddish borders appear directly on the pods. Treatment: Never touch or harvest beans when plants are wet, as water spreads the fungus. Rotate crops annually. Remove infected pods immediately. Spraying a mixture of baking soda and water (1 tsp per liter) or a bio-fungicide like Trichoderma can protect new young pods from developing these spots.

While usually on leaves, in severe cases, the white powdery growth covers the pods, causing them to malform and dry out. Treatment: Spray a mixture of milk and water (1:9 ratio) in bright sunlight; it acts as a natural fungicide. Dusting the plants with sulphur powder is very effective. Prune dense foliage to ensure sunlight reaches the pods.

Rust-colored pustules appear on the pods, making them unsightly and weak. Prune plants to ensure sunlight reaches the interior. Clear away fallen debris where spores hide. Avoid wetting the foliage when watering. Dusting plants with sulphur powder or spraying a wettable sulphur solution is a common organic treatment. Early detection and removal of affected parts can save the rest of the crop.

Reddish-brown, powdery pustules form on the pods, making them look dirty and unappealing. Treatment: Avoid wetting the pods when watering. Prune the plant to allow sunlight to hit the pods (sunlight kills the spores). Dusting with sulphur powder is a common organic remedy. Remove severely infected plant parts to save the rest of the crop.

A white, cottony growth appears on the pods, especially near the soil or where pods touch each other. The pod eventually turns into a soft, watery mush. Treatment: Space plants widely to ensure the soil surface dries out. Mulch with straw to keep pods off the damp soil. Remove any rotting pods immediately. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which creates dense, humid canopies that mold loves.

The pods become mottled (light and dark green patches), shiny, and malformed/bumpy. They are tough and fibrous to eat. Treatment: There is no cure for the virus. Remove and destroy the infected plant immediately. The virus is spread by aphids, so control them using yellow sticky traps or insecticidal soap sprays. Plant virus-resistant varieties like "Arka Komal" (for French beans).

This is caused by a Boron deficiency, not a germ. The internal flesh develops hard, black, corky spots, and the center may rot. Dissolve 1 teaspoon of Borax powder in 5 liters of water and water the soil to replenish Boron. Ensure regular watering, as dry soil prevents the roots from absorbing nutrients. Add plenty of compost before the next planting season to balance the soil.

Similar to potatoes, corky spots appear on the root surface. Keep the soil moisture consistent; do not let it dry out during root development. Avoid using fresh manure, which can harbor the bacteria. Lower soil pH slightly if possible, as scab thrives in alkaline soil. Rotate crops and avoid planting beets in the same spot for three years.

Rough, raised, corky patches appear on the beet skin. It doesn't affect the taste much but ruins the texture and storage life. Treatment: Scab bacteria thrive in dry, alkaline soil. Keep the soil consistently moist, especially during the first 6 weeks of growth. Avoid using fresh manure or wood ash (which raises pH) immediately before planting. Rotate crops; do not plant beets where potatoes grew recently.

Bright orange/red beetles chew holes in the leaves, especially young seedlings. Treatment: They are sluggish in the early morning; handpick and destroy them. Dust wood ash or red chilli powder mixed with flour on the leaves to repel them. Deep plow the soil after harvest to kill grubs.

The main root becomes stunted, deformed, and covered in small bumps (galls) or excessive hairy side roots. Treatment: Plant marigolds densely in the bed one season before planting beets, as their roots release chemicals that repel nematodes. Add neem cake to the soil to encourage beneficial microbes. Practice a 3-year crop rotation. Solarize the soil in summer (cover moist soil with clear plastic) if the infestation is heavy.

The root turns black and mushy, often starting at the "shoulder" (top) or the tip. This usually happens in wet, heavy clay soils. Treatment: Improve soil drainage; do not plant in waterlogged areas. Use raised beds to keep the soil drier. Thin the seedlings early so they aren't crowded. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately. A copper-based fungicide drench can help if applied early.

You may see sawdust-like powder at the base of the tree or on the trunk. A grub is tunneling inside. Treatment: Locate the hole on the trunk. Insert a stiff wire to kill the larva inside. Seal the hole with a paste of wet clay and neem oil. Keep the tree base clean of debris.

These caterpillars hide in the soil during the day and eat the top of the root or chew through the stem at night. Treatment: Dig around the base of the damaged plant to find and kill the greyish caterpillar. Place a "collar" (a paper cup with the bottom cut out) around young seedlings to protect the stem. Crushed eggshells sprinkled around the plant base can deter them.
Round spots with reddish margins on leaves. Loss of leaves results in small, woody roots. Thin plants to improve airflow. Apply copper fungicide or Neem oil. Rotate crops every 3 years.
Rough, corky, brown spots on the root surface. Do not use fresh manure; use well-rotted compost. Keep soil moisture consistent. Acidic soil reduces scab (avoid over-liming).
